title: Failed-Part Bounty for Insurance Subrogation
one_liner: Pay plumbers a bounty to bag, photograph and chain-of-custody the pipe, supply line or fitting that failed, then sell the evidence and a brand-level failure database to insurers' subrogation units and manufacturers.
customer: Subrogation departments and subro vendors at regional and mutual homeowners insurers (the ones too small to send a forensic engineer to a $9k supply-line loss). Second buyers: plumbing manufacturers, distributors and private-label buyers who license the failure data.
problem: Water damage is among the top two homeowner claim categories. Product-defect subrogation (a supply line, PEX fitting, toilet connector, ice-maker line or water heater that failed early) only works if someone kept the failed part. The plumber is on scene 1 to 3 days before the adjuster, cuts the failed piece out, and tosses it in the truck-bed scrap bin. When the adjuster arrives the evidence is gone, the insurer eats the loss, and the manufacturer's lawyers cite spoliation. Insurers only hire the $2,000 forensic engineer on the big losses, so the routine $8-15k losses are never pursued. Meanwhile every plumber knows which brands are failing (certain plastic-nut braided lines, certain fill valves, certain fitting lots) but nobody aggregates it.
solution: A 90-second protocol and kit. Tamper-evident bag with a QR label, a phone flow (photo of the part in place, photo after removal, the manufacturer stamp or date code, homeowner e-signature by text, and the claim number if one exists). A weekly courier pickup from the shop and a climate-controlled evidence locker. Optional one-page factual cause-of-loss statement drawn from the same photos (sudden burst versus long-term seepage, which is exactly the 'gradual leak' exclusion that decides whether homeowners get paid). Every part is logged by brand, model, date code and failure mode, which builds a Backblaze-style public failure-rate report by product line. Insurers get the part plus a ready evidence package. The shop gets a bounty and a small line item on the invoice.
why_now: Water-loss severity has risen sharply and carriers are under pressure on homeowners loss ratios, so they are hunting for recovery dollars. Copper and steel tariffs plus the shift to PEX and imported fittings have flooded the market with cheaper components of unknown quality. Photo and OCR tooling now makes a cheap, standardized evidence workflow possible, and the subrogation trade press is openly saying evidence preservation is the make-or-break step.
revenue_model: Insurer or subro vendor pays $75-150 per part with a documented chain of custody, of which $40-60 goes to the shop and tech. Plus a 3-8% success share on any recovery that follows. Plus annual data licenses ($15-60k) to manufacturers, distributors and big-box private-label buyers, and per-report fees for expert-witness-ready packages.
non_obvious_insight: The evidence that decides tens of millions in recoveries is currently destroyed daily by the only people who touch it first, and the reason is not malice. Nobody pays a tech to spend 4 minutes and a bag on a piece of scrap. The plumber, not the adjuster, is the true first-notice-of-loss for the product itself. The bounty is a price signal, and the dataset that falls out is one nobody else can buy.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 shops through a local PHCC chapter and the owner Facebook and peer groups with a flat $50 per bag and a free kit. Design the label and the phone flow in a form tool. Collect the first 50 parts with photos. Take the first 20 case files to two regional mutual insurers and a subrogation vendor and ask them which they would have pursued. Sell a paid pilot for 100 parts on the strength of their answers.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Donan Engineering - Loss Logistics, Envista Forensics and Rimkus (forensic engineering / property loss consulting), LeakBot, ServiceTitan and CompanyCam (plumber field software). White space: Caveat: the session's WebSearch budget ran out (200 of 200) before any search ran. This verdict rests on direct page fetches of about a dozen vendor, industry and government sites, plus two empty GitHub searches. I did not check Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or trade press, so I could not rule out a small funded startup doing exactly this. Run 4-6 searches before committing money. Suggested queries: 'subrogation evidence preservation plumber', 'failed part bounty', 'water loss evidence kit', and the same on Crunchbase.

What I found is a real gap in what I could reach. Evidence logistics and forensic engineering exist for engineer-assigned losses (Donan, Envista, Rimkus). Insurer-funded plumber networks exist (LeakBot). Plumber field software exists (ServiceTitan, CompanyCam). No page I read describes any of these paying or equipping the plumber to retain the failed part on routine sub-$15k water losses. The public failure data I found is weak (SaferProducts.gov). Nothing I found is a date-code and brand-level failure-rate dataset.

Unserved specifically: (1) plumber-side capture at the moment of removal, including a per-part payment. (2) A neutral custodian and evidence package for the $8-15k tier, which is below the point where a $2k engineer is dispatched. (3) A structured brand, model and date-code failure dataset from real removed parts.

The main risks are structural, not competitive. (a) The plumber often arrives before a claim exists, so the claim number and the bounty payer are unknown at bagging. (b) Mitigation contractors and insurer-dispatched vendors may reach the site first on many losses. (c) The recovery economics of small product-defect claims are unproven, so insurers may not pay $75-150 for parts they would not pursue anyway. (d) A public brand-level failure report invites manufacturer legal pushback. (e) A 'cause-of-loss statement' from a tech risks unlicensed-engineering objections. (f) I could not fetch HomeServe (403), so I cannot say whether that plumber-network incumbent already does something like this.

title: Scribe-Safe Billing: White-Label Audit for Billing Companies
one_liner: Outsourced billing companies buy a per-provider, coder-signed drift monitor and quarterly attestation letter, then resell it to their small-practice clients as 'scribe-safe billing'.
customer: Mid-size outsourced billing and RCM companies (roughly 40-500 providers under management, spread across 5-50 small groups, for example HBMA members) that bill for practices using a mix of scribes. Later channels: practice-management and EHR marketplaces, and IPAs.
problem: The bulk of scribe adoption in small practices is cheap or low-cost tooling with no compliance officer behind it. The billing company sees every claim across many clients and scribe vendors, is paid a percentage of collections (so scribe uplift raises its own fee), and can be exposed as a party that caused false claims. Its contract says the client owns documentation, but that does not stop a payer or DOJ from asking the biller what it did. Enterprise audit platforms are priced and sold for organizations with in-house compliance staff, so this segment gets nothing. Small groups also lack the resources to appeal payer downcodes.
solution: 'Scribe-Safe' program the biller white-labels. (1) Claims-only monitor across the biller's whole book, with no EHR access: per-provider E/M and modifier drift versus specialty peers, plus the payer downcode rate from 835 remits (CARC 150, 'payer deems the information does not support this level of service') as a leading signal. (2) Quarterly coder-signed review of about 8 encounters per flagged provider, focused on MDM and total-time statements. (3) A signed quarterly attestation letter per practice that the biller can show a client, payer or auditor. (4) A contract addendum plus a refund workflow so findings reach the practice's designated contact and can be acted on within the 60-day overpayment rule, so the biller never sits on an identified problem. (5) Cross-book benchmark by scribe vendor and specialty returned to the biller as a sales asset.
why_now: Small groups adopted low-cost scribes in 2025-26, payers' automated downcoding programs are now hitting the small groups least able to appeal, outsourced billing keeps growing, and billing companies compete on differentiation as AI coding commoditizes their core work. Law-firm commentary warns that 'the AI suggested it' is not a defense. Billing companies now need something independent to point to.
revenue_model: Wholesale $12-20 per provider per month; the biller resells at $25-40 or bundles it for retention. $25 per encounter for extra coder reviews. A 300-provider biller is about $45-70k a year, so 25 billers is roughly $1.1-1.75M ARR. Coder time is about $7 per provider per month at 8 reviews per quarter of about 6 minutes each with an AI pre-read, giving 55-65% gross margin. Land through a 60-day paid pilot at $4-6k per biller.
non_obvious_insight: The payer's own downcode rate is a free, externally labeled audit signal. A jump in CARC 150 adjustments for one provider after go-live means the payer's model has already flagged the notes, before any human looks. The billing company is also the only actor with a cross-client, cross-scribe view, and it buys cover more than detection: an independent signature is the product, which is why more AI coding automation is not a substitute.
first_30_days: Contact HBMA chapter leaders and 40 billing-company owners on LinkedIn. Offer a 60-day paid pilot ($4-6k) that starts with a scan of the biller's aggregated 12-month 837/835 book, structured under the biller's counsel and with the findings routed to practices, not left with the biller. Recruit 2 CPC/CPMA contractors and a healthcare lawyer to draft the addendum and refund workflow. Deliver a provider watchlist and 30 coder-signed reviews to each pilot. Goal: 3 signed pilots and 1 conversion to a per-provider contract.

competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: VMG Health (Compliance Risk Analyzer + AI Governance and Targeted Coding Audits), MDaudit, Healthicity (Audit Manager, Compliance Manager, E/M Analyzer/Utilization Benchmarking tool), Ambience Healthcare (scribe vendor with coding). White space: Nobody I found sells a scribe-specific, independent, coder-signed audit product. The gaps are: (1) An explicit before/after go-live drift baseline per provider, benchmarked against specialty peers and other scribe adopters. VMG's Compliance Risk Analyzer and Healthicity's E/M benchmarking do peer outlier analysis but are not framed around scribe go-live cohorts. (2) A review protocol built around what fails audits under the 2021 E/M rules: MDM and time attestations, not HPI/exam bloat. None of the vendor pages I read describe this. (3) An audit memo designed to be handed to a payer, auditor or OIG, plus a payer-downcoding forecast. (4) Independence from the scribe vendor, since Ambience, Abridge and DeepScribe all self-attest coding quality. (5) Scribe-agnostic coverage across a mixed-vendor group. Several legal write-ups recommend exactly the 'post-implementation baseline audit comparing AI-generated coding patterns against prior practice' (https://www.subjecttoinquiry.com/2026/06/ai-assisted-billing-could-create-fca-pitfalls-how-healthcare-companies-can-get-ahead-of-risk/), and none of the articles I read named a vendor that sells it. Caveat: this is a wedge in framing and packaging, not a technology moat. The existing audit firms and platforms (VMG, MDaudit, Healthicity) can run this same claims analysis and coder review, and could rebrand it 'AI scribe audit' within a quarter or two. My search was also incomplete, and startups from 2026 may exist that I did not surface. | How this version avoids them: VMG Health, MDaudit and Healthicity sell audit software and consulting to enterprises with compliance departments, so their pricing, seat model and sales cycle do not fit a 5-provider clinic served by a biller. We sell wholesale through the biller instead. A follow-up search found Charta Health (AI pre-bill chart review against 2021 E/M rules) and Combine Health (AI appeals and revenue-integrity agents). These are software that adds more AI to coding and appeals. They do not give an independent signature, do not verify time statements, and do not read the whole book by scribe cohort. title: Serial Match: AP-Only Recovery for Exchange Buyers
one_liner: A success-fee audit that takes one accounts-payable export from an independent rotable pool or Part 145 station, finds money its repair vendors already owe, and collects it. It starts with credits the vendor has already conceded, then moves to repeat-failure claims.
customer: Independent rotable exchange pools, parts resellers and Part 145 stations that buy a few hundred outsourced repairs and exchange units a year from 10 or more shops, roughly $5-40M of repair spend (my assumption, unverified). The buyer is the Controller or VP Materials at a firm with a 2-4 person back office. These firms sit outside power-by-the-hour contracts, so the warranty exposure is theirs. They multi-source on price, so they have little vendor-relationship fear. They also see the same serial number pass through many hands. Regionals, EMS operators and lessors are phase 2.
problem: The parent idea had four named weaknesses: PBH and maintenance-plan contracts remove warranty exposure for many small fleets, integrating with each operator's maintenance system is hard, fear of annoying the shop, and no proof anyone pays. A pool has none of these. Its serialized units cycle through repair invoices, exchange credits and core returns. The same P/N and S/N can appear on two invoices from one shop within the warranty window, and nobody joins invoice lines by serial number. Beside that sit credit memos issued but never applied, core credits not netted, no-fault-found evaluation fees on in-warranty units, and turnaround guarantees never credited. Pool gross margins are thin, so recovering 1-3% of repair spend moves EBITDA. The warranty windows are short and full of exclusions, so recovery has to be systematic, with a claim filed for every eligible unit.
solution: Input is one vendor-ledger export plus the invoice PDFs, with no maintenance-system integration. An LLM extractor builds a serial-level table: P/N (including interchangeable P/Ns), S/N, repair date, charges and the warranty text printed on the invoice or PO. Recovery runs in three passes, ordered from least to most disputed. Pass 1 is zero-dispute money: open and unapplied credit memos, duplicate payments, and core credits not applied. Pass 2 is the repeat-serial detector: the same S/N back to the same shop inside its window, plus the same S/N failing after different shops' repairs. Pass 3 is contested items: NFF fees on in-warranty units and turnaround-guarantee credits. Claims go out on each vendor's own form. A vendor playbook library covers the top 60 shops: warranty terms, exclusions, contacts, average days to credit and past acceptance rate. We chase every claim to a posted credit or cash. Phase 2 adds read-only receiving and removal data from the customer's ERP to confirm failures the invoices alone can't show.
why_now: Reliable, cheap LLM extraction from messy repair-invoice PDFs and warranty fine print is what makes an AP-only audit viable. Before 2025 it needed offshore data-entry teams, which killed contingency margins. Aftermarket parts prices and repair turn times have also climbed since the 2022-23 supply squeeze (my assumption, unverified). That makes each exchange unit worth more, so pools tie up more capital in them and each unclaimed failure costs more.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 20% of cash and credits recovered, or 25% on contested pass-3 items, with a 12-month tail after the audit. The fee is due only when cash arrives or the credit is applied, not when the memo is issued. That solves the objection to paying cash on a credit the customer can only spend at that shop. There is no upfront cost and no minimum. Year 2 adds a $2-4k/month continuous-monitoring tier for pools with over $15M of spend. Anonymized vendor-acceptance and turn-time data is a later product.
non_obvious_insight: Sequence matters more than segment. Leading with credits the vendor has already conceded gives first cash in 3-4 weeks, with no dispute and no relationship risk. That builds the trust to file contested claims later. Every contested claim, won or lost, adds to the playbook library: per-shop acceptance rates, exclusion language and time to credit. That library is the cornered resource and process power a generalist cannot copy. The pool is also the freight-audit shipper of aviation: high invoice volume, many vendors, serial-tracked goods and no reason to protect any single vendor.
first_30_days: Build a target list of about 60 pools and Part 145 stations from public repair-station and trade-association directories. Send 40 direct outreach messages offering a free scan: they send 12 months of vendor ledger and invoices, and we return the dollars found within 10 business days. The only thing we ask for is permission to file. Hire a retired warranty or materials coordinator as a paid advisor for vendor quirks. Close 3 audits and deliver ranked claim lists. File pass-1 claims first and aim for the first credit memo by day 30. Set an explicit kill test: if the median first-pass yield is under 1% of repair spend across the first 5 files, stop or narrow the segment. Publish the aggregate finding, such as the share of eligible repeat repairs never claimed, as the lead magnet.

title: Federal-Agreement Lab for State SNAP QC Reviewers
one_liner: Sell calibration drills to the small, high-leverage group whose findings set the official error rate, the state QC reviewers, scoring them against a federal answer key and putting part of the fee at risk on the state-federal disagreement rate.
customer: State SNAP Quality Control unit directors and the state SNAP directors who sponsor them, in the 41 states above 6% that must now file remediation plans. Each QC unit is a few dozen reviewers. Warm lead: Alabama DHR, which posted an RFP for 'SNAP Quality Control review assessment and training'. Check who won and at what scope. Targets: states within about 1 point of a tier line, once the FY2025 state table is pulled.
problem: The official rate is not the state's own number. USDA re-reviews a subsample and adjusts (regresses) the state's findings, and disputed differences go to arbitration. Rates are cliffs (6/8/10%), each worth tens to hundreds of millions in state benefit cost. A state QC reviewer who under-calls errors gets corrected upward by federal re-review. One who over-calls inflates the state's own rate. QC units are small and turnover-prone, and the FNS 310 handbook is dense. Today that calibration happens ad hoc, in meetings or through occasional consultants.
solution: A library of about 200 synthetic completed-review packets: case file, interview notes and an 'as-reviewed' finding, with planted misses and planted false alarms. Answer keys are adjudicated by retired FNS and state reviewers and cite FNS 310 sections. Reviewers find the errors, and we score agreement with the key by element (income, household composition, shelter, resources, ABAWD/H.R.1 rules), by reviewer and by supervisor. We add weekly live calibration sessions run by the retired reviewers, and an arbitration-readiness checklist. We do not perform QC reviews. We train and score, which keeps us clear of the federal oversight rules for third-party QC contractors (verify against the 2018 Farm Bill provisions). Method is symmetric: the goal is agreement with the federal standard, not lower error counts.
why_now: FY2025 rates came out June 24, 2026: 41 states above 6% and a 10.62% national rate. FY2026 rates finalize through federal re-review and arbitration into mid-2027, and states can use the better of FY2025 and FY2026 for FY2028. The FY2027 sample opens Oct 1, 2026 and sets FY2030 cost share. H.R.1 made every QC finding a budget line, so QC directors now have executive attention and remediation-plan deadlines. The Alabama RFP shows states already buy QC-side assessment and training.
revenue_model: $90-250k per state QC unit per year: about $2.5-4k per reviewer seat, a packet-library license and quarterly calibration sessions. 20-25% of the fee is at risk, refunded if the state-federal difference rate on FNS re-reviewed cases does not narrow. FNS measures that outcome, not us. 41 states at 40% penetration is about $5-8M ARR, so the ceiling is small but each logo is high-value and fast to close. Expansion: Medicaid eligibility-error programs (H.R.1 adds payment reductions starting around FY2030, verify), plus a per-case add-on for arbitration memo review. Prices are unvalidated assumptions.
non_obvious_insight: Dollars at stake per trained head is 100-1000x higher for QC reviewers than for eligibility workers. A 30-person unit's calibration can swing a tier cliff worth $100M+, and a county worker's cannot. The regressed rate turns under-calling into a hidden tax, not good luck. Unlike eligibility policy, which varies by state, QC review method is national (FNS 310), so one packet library serves every state. That fixes the parent's per-state case-library cost problem. The buyer population is tiny, homogeneous and reachable through a few networks.
first_30_days: Days 1-5: pull the Alabama RFP, announcement and results documents to learn the winner, scope and price. Recruit 2 retired state or FNS QC reviewers as adjudicators at $100-150 an hour. Days 5-18: write 25 planted-error packets from the public FNS 310 handbook and published arbitration guidance. Days 10-30: reach 15 QC directors through APHSA payment-accuracy contacts and FNS regional liaisons. Offer a free blind 10-packet test for 5 of their reviewers and return an agreement-gap report within a week. Convert 1-2 to $25-40k pilots via simplified procurement.

title: Power Passport: Scoring Dead Factories on Amps, Permits
one_liner: A database and paid inspection report that rates shuttered Midwest plants on the things reshoring manufacturers actually need (utility service, slab, crane, transferable air and discharge permits) instead of square footage.
customer: Reshoring manufacturers and their site-selection consultants (first buyer). Industrial listing brokers and sellers of dead factories (they pay to differentiate their listings). Regional economic-development bodies and utility economic-development teams (annual license).
problem: Brokers list buildings by square feet, clear height and dock doors. A reshoring plant needs enough energized 480V/13.2kV capacity, a slab that can carry presses and large CNCs, crane rails, and a transferable Ohio EPA air permit for a paint or wash line. Greenfield permitting and long-lead transformers and switchgear can add 9-18 months before the first good part. Meanwhile data-center developers are hunting the same brownfield shells for their existing utility service, so the buildings that suit manufacturing are disappearing without either side understanding what was in them.
solution: Build a parcel-level dataset of pre-2005 industrial buildings across Ohio, Pennsylvania, Michigan and Indiana by combining public air and wastewater permit records, county parcel data, utility maps, aerial imagery for crane bays and rail spurs, and Phase I history. Score each building on power, permits, structure and contamination risk. Sell a 'Power Passport': a 12-page report with a licensed industrial electrician's walk-through, gear nameplate photos, permit transferability notes and utility will-serve context, delivered in 5 days.
why_now: The 2026 reshoring wave and the data-center land grab are competing for the same shells. Transformer and switchgear lead times are still measured in many months to years. The gap between what manufacturers need and what listings say is at its widest, and brokers have no tooling to fill it.
revenue_model: $1.5k-$3.5k per Passport (paid by the broker or seller, or by the buyer). A 0.5%-1% success fee on closed industrial deals. $25k-$60k per year data licences to economic-development agencies, utilities and site-selection firms. Later, a capital vehicle that buys the best shells and subdivides them into permitted multi-tenant 'factory condos'.
non_obvious_insight: In a dead Ohio plant the building is the cheapest part. The energized service, the paper permits and the crane rails are the asset, and they are invisible to anyone who has not tried to open a factory. Every reshorer I know lost most of a year to power and permits, not to hiring.
first_30_days: Pick one metro (Akron/Canton or the Mahoning Valley). Pull public Ohio EPA permit records and county parcel data to list 150 candidate buildings. Hire an electrician for 20 walk-throughs at about $150 per hour. Cold-call 25 industrial listing brokers offering a free first Passport in exchange for a testimonial and a right to the data. Convert 3-5 into paying $1.5k reports and one economic-development office into a pilot licence.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Brownfield.ai, Scout (ScoutCities), LandGate, Enverus Site & Screen. White space: Nobody I found productises a building-level, physically verified 'inside-the-fence' record for dead Midwest plants. That record would cover the electrician-verified main service size, voltage, gear age and nameplates, spare capacity, slab and crane-rail condition, the state of the existing air and wastewater permits, and a utility will-serve letter, all in a scored, comparable format sold before the deal. The funded players (LandGate, Enverus, GridCARE, Paces) work at the substation and grid level and are aimed at data centers. Utility and state databases (JobsOhio, AEP, FirstEnergy, ZoomProspector) verify sites and utility service, not building gear or permit status. Scout and Brownfield.ai are the closest competitors, but they look desktop- and network-led with no per-building inspection, and I found no evidence they carry electrician-verified data. The genuine gap is a trusted, standardised, seller-commissioned building electrical and permit record, not the parcel-scoring layer, which is already crowded and funded. The idea's weaker points: the Ohio permit-transferability wedge is thin (see evidence), and it is unproven that brokers will pay $1.5k-$3.5k.

title: Referee Sampling for Black Mass and Battery Scrap
one_liner: Independent sampling and assay of black mass lots, using Pierre Gy's Theory of Sampling from mining, so scrap sellers and recyclers stop fighting over 5-15% payable swings.
customer: Battery-scrap sellers who are paid by assay: gigafactory scrap desks, EV and ESS dismantlers, and shredder pre-processors in Germany, Poland, the US Midwest, Ontario and Korea. Buyers are hydromet recyclers and trading houses that want defensible acceptance. Whoever needs the settlement pays $1.5-4k per lot or $15-40 per tonne, and often splits it.
problem: Black mass is a worst-case heterogeneous powder: coarse Cu and Al foil flakes, plastic, residual electrolyte, graphite, and a nugget effect for Ni, Co and Cu. Payables are computed on the assay of a few grams. Anyone from mining knows 90% or more of assay error is sampling error (fundamental, segregation and grouping errors), not lab error. Sellers and buyers each sample their own way and get 5-15% differences on Ni, Co and Li. Disputes are settled by splitting the difference or sending to an 'umpire' lab that repeats the same bad sampling. On a $60-150k lot, that swing is $5-15k of pure noise, paid to whoever wins the argument. The industry's chemists treat it like a homogeneous chemical.
solution: Build a containerised, safety-rated sampling and sample-prep station (dryer, rotary divider, splitter, pulverizer, inert handling) and a written ToS-based protocol: incremental sampling from a falling stream or drum auger, particle-size and moisture control, and duplicate-sample bias checks. Send splits to an accredited lab and issue a 'referee certificate' with a stated sampling variance. Provide a two-line settlement clause template that buyer and seller adopt (for example, 'referee result binds') and tie lot IDs to the recycled-content and material-recovery documentation the EU Battery Regulation requires. Extend later to PCB e-waste, catalyst scrap and mixed copper scrap.
why_now: Black mass volumes are ramping with European and US gigafactory ramp-up scrap (often 10-30% early yield loss). EU regulation is pushing black mass toward hazardous-waste treatment and export limits, and Battery Regulation recovery and recycled-content rules are phasing in. Several Western recyclers restructured or were bought out in 2025 (Li-Cycle into Glencore, for example), so sellers now fear counterparty and assay risk. Payables have become the main margin lever as Co and Ni prices swing.
revenue_model: Per-lot referee fee ($1.5-4k) or $15-40 per tonne, annual retainers for large scrap generators, leasing or operating sample-prep stations at recycler gates, and certification and training for recyclers' in-house sampling.
non_obvious_insight: The fight looks like an assay-accuracy problem but it is a sampling problem, and the solution is 1950s-1990s sampling theory that only mining and metallurgy people internalise. Recycling companies are staffed by chemists and process engineers who sample like it is a solution. A person who has been burned by a bad grade-control sample sees the whole market as one giant unsampled stockpile.
first_30_days: Rent time on a commercial sample-prep lab or buy used splitting and pulverizing gear (about $40-60k). Offer a free duplicate-sampling study to three scrap generators or dismantlers: take 10 lots, sample each with the seller's method and yours, and send blind splits to two labs. Show them the between-protocol bias, then sell a 6-month referee retainer. A local mining-lab partner and one senior sampling consultant give instant credibility.

title: Nonrenewal Desk for Colorado Independent Agencies
one_liner: An agent-side triage-and-evidence service that starts when a Front Range nonrenewal or score-disclosure notice lands, and charges most of its fee only when the policy is saved.
customer: Owner-principals of independent insurance agencies in Boulder, Jefferson, Larimer, El Paso and Douglas counties. Each has 150+ wildland-urban-interface homeowner policies, is appointed with 6 or more carriers so it can re-market, and has received several nonrenewals or surcharge notices since January 2026. Colorado only. California is dropped until AB 75 is confirmed enacted.
problem: When a nonrenewal or score disclosure arrives, the agent has about 10 days to get an acknowledgement and about 30 days to a decision (HB25-1182). The agent has no verified evidence, and the free homeowner kits (FireRisk.ai, Defensible Space Score) only produce letters. A corrected score may not move the premium, because insurers can meet the law with a manual mitigation discount and do not have to accept third-party imagery. The agent loses the commission and the bundled auto and umbrella policies, roughly $600 a year or more per WUI household.
solution: The agent forwards the notice PDF and gets three things within 48 hours. (1) A Lot Ledger: dated 15-50 cm imagery and public lidar canopy and clearance measurements set against each feature the insurer disclosed. Each feature is marked contradicted, confirmed or unknowable. (2) A Credit Map: for each carrier the agency is appointed with, which filed mitigation credits or underwriting-exception paths the evidence supports, so the pack asks for the premium or retention outcome and not just a score change. (3) A carrier-formatted pack timed to the 10 and 30 day clocks, plus a re-marketing shortlist when the appeal is weak. The desk declines to file when the evidence does not contradict the score. That keeps the concession ledger clean and makes carriers trust the packs. After trust is built, the same imagery layer is run across the agency's whole WUI book to flag likely errors before renewal.
why_now: HB25-1182 has been in force since July 1, 2026, so disclosures, appeals and the 10/30-day clocks are now real for every Colorado WUI policy. Independent agents are the ones absorbing the nonrenewals. Public regional aerial flights, USGS-style lidar and cheap commercial archives mean the first appeals need no imagery licence. I did not verify that insurer appeal desks are unprepared, so the plan does not rely on it; the trigger is the notice itself.
revenue_model: $249 per month per agency, including 5 triage runs and a book scan of up to 300 WUI policies. Extra packs are $149 each. A flat $300 success fee applies per policy retained or re-marketed within 90 days of a pack. There is no percentage of premium, to avoid producer-compensation and rebating problems. At 20 agencies, that is about $60k in subscriptions plus roughly $90k in success fees, around $150k ARR, with gross margin above 70% once imagery is bought per filed case only.
non_obvious_insight: The product is a decision about what will actually change the outcome: fix the input, harden the house, or re-market it. It is not a rebuttal letter. Honest triage is the moat, because a desk that refuses weak cases gets a higher concession rate, and a concession ledger keyed by carrier, vendor, input error and evidence type becomes something carriers cannot get elsewhere. Carrier-side vendors like Zesty, Nearmap and Cotality cannot sell against their own customers' scores. That is counter-positioning.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 Front Range agencies through a Colorado independent-agent association or by direct outreach to principals. Run concierge delivery by hand with an analyst using public imagery, lidar and QGIS, with no licensing. Give the first 5 files per agency free and charge $99 from file 6. Aim for 40 real notices and 20 filed appeals with outcomes tracked. Send agencies a private weekly concession scoreboard as the sales asset.

title: Bridge Loans for Medicare Drug-Price Refunds
one_liner: Fund the 3-4 week float independent pharmacies now carry on Medicare's negotiated-price drugs, underwritten on predictable refund data, before Ozempic joins the list in January.
customer: Independent pharmacies with senior-heavy books, especially those serving long-term care, then 5-50 store groups and PSAOs. Average exposure is estimated at over $27,000 a month per community pharmacy.
problem: Since January 1, 2026, pharmacies pay wholesalers full price for Eliquis, Jardiance, Xarelto, Farxiga, Januvia, Entresto and others, dispense at Medicare's Maximum Fair Price, and wait weeks for the difference to arrive through the Medicare Transaction Facilitator. Estimates put the float at $27k+ a month for the average community pharmacy, over $500M a month industry-wide, on top of wholesalers who still auto-debit weekly. On thin margins that is a real solvency risk. Banks see a pharmacy, not an insured refund.
solution: Start with a reconciliation tool that ingests the pharmacy's PMS claims export and the MTF remittance files and shows late or missing refunds. Then offer a non-recourse advance of about 90% of the expected refund on each week's MFP claims, repaid from the actual MTF payment through a controlled deposit account or sweep. Confirm with CMS and the facilitator what payment-routing options exist, and fall back to a bank-account sweep if third-party routing is not allowed.
why_now: The program only became real on January 1, 2026, and it is already causing cash-flow warnings from pharmacy coalitions. On January 1, 2027, 15 more drugs join, including semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, Rybelsus), which multiplies the float. Wholesalers have not yet solved it and the bank market does not understand it, so there is a window of a few quarters before someone standardizes the answer.
revenue_model: A fee of about 1-1.75% per advance cycle, which works out to roughly 15-25% annualized, plus a $99 a month reconciliation subscription. Contingency of about 10% on missing refunds recovered. Later, sell or syndicate the receivables to a credit fund.
non_obvious_insight: To a bank this looks like distress lending to a struggling small business. In reality it is close to prime paper: the obligor is a drug manufacturer with a statutory duty to pay, routed through a federal facilitator, backed by claim-level data. Only someone who knows how PMS claims map to MFP eligibility, and how a reversal or dispute can claw a refund back, can underwrite it. The free reconciliation report is the wedge that gets the data before any money goes out.
first_30_days: Offer a free 'find my missing refunds' report to 25 pharmacies through state association newsletters and pharmacy owner Facebook groups. Line up a $500k credit line from a regional bank or family office and keep the first ten advances small. Talk to a fintech attorney about commercial-financing disclosure laws by state. Approach one PSAO about distribution.

Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SpendMend (MFP Rebate Reconciliation), Plenful (MFP Intelligence / MFP Command Center), ScriptPro Financial Advantage, Liberty Software (and other PMS vendors, e.g. PioneerRx, PrimeRx, Redsail). White space: Verdict: gap, and a narrow one. In roughly 27 searches across varied terms (MFP refund advance, bridge loan, factoring, fintech, PSAO program, wholesaler program) I found NO product that specifically underwrites and advances against MTF-remitted MFP refunds. Pharmacy lenders sell generic A/R and MCA lines, and the MFP players only sell reconciliation. The unserved space is a claim-level underwriting and servicing capability for refund dilution risk: 340B lesser-of rejections (RARC N907 inappropriate rejections), reversals, Good Faith Inquiry disputes, and authorized-generic refund amounts. It is most valuable for borrowers whose float is large: LTC/senior-care pharmacies, 5-50 store groups, and possibly 340B covered entities in the HRSA rebate pilot, where the float is $8.9M-$208M a year for hospitals (Health Affairs). It also applies to the January 2027 step-up when semaglutide joins.

The wedge is weak in five ways.
1. The 'free missing-refund report' is already crowded: SpendMend, Plenful ($76M raised), ScriptPro, Liberty, and free Beacon MFP dashboards.
2. A typical independent's float is small, about $11k a week or $27k a month per NCPA. At 15-25% APR that is roughly $4-7k a year of gross revenue per pharmacy, before losses and a cost of funds of 8-10%. Customer acquisition through state associations and Facebook groups will be costly relative to that.
3. Wholesalers control the payment path. Cardinal routes MFP refunds through Central Pay and wholesalers auto-debit weekly, so a lender's sweep sits behind the wholesaler in practice. Cardinal customers cannot easily direct refunds to a lender-controlled account.
4. 'Non-recourse' is hard to deliver. Manufacturers can reverse refunds and CMS's own materials describe reversals when claims prove ineligible, so a lender will need pharmacy recourse or holdbacks. That undermines the 'prime paper' insight.
5. Policy is a moving target. CMS made manufacturers include cash-flow mitigation plans in their MFP effectuation plans (accelerated refunds, self-identification). NCPA is still pushing CMS and manufacturers for faster payment, including in Sept 2026 comments on the 2028 guidance.

Adjacent generic lenders can also just add MFP refunds to a borrowing base.

title: Escrow and Assay Settlement House for Scrap
one_liner: A neutral settlement house that holds the buyer's money in a licensed escrow and the sealed sample in a vault, then releases payment automatically on the assay of record. It starts with black mass and grows into a registry, financing and an index.
customer: Two sides. Sellers are mid-size dismantlers and pre-processors who fear both assay games and recycler insolvency after the 2025 restructurings. Buyers are recyclers who want to win feed, especially weakly capitalised or new-capacity ones that can rent credibility from a neutral escrow. The first anchor is one buyer signing our Standard Settlement Terms, which opens every one of its sellers at once. A buyer pays half the fee.
problem: The parent sells arbitration after the fight, once, to a price-sensitive party in trouble. Sellers actually face two bundled anxieties on every lot. One is assay noise or bias. The other is credit exposure on the assay-based final payment, unsecured for weeks and frozen if the lot is disputed. After Li-Cycle's sale to Glencore and other 2025 restructurings, sellers price that risk by discounting or refusing weaker buyers. Nobody sells both fixes in one contract. Banks' letters of credit and provisional payments cover part of the credit side, and assay disputes are left to umpire clauses.
solution: Sold within six months as a Settle-in-14-days contract pack. It is a tri-party agreement (buyer, seller, us) drafted once by a trade-finance law firm. A licensed escrow agent or bank partner holds funds, and we never hold money or inventory. A certified crew takes a sealed triplicate sample-of-record at the seller's dock. One split goes to a pre-agreed accredited lab, and two are stored in a third-party vault. Payment releases by formula, payable times assay-of-record, with no ex-post negotiation. Only if the retained splits differ beyond the pre-agreed Gy variance tolerance is the third split assayed. Later layers are these. (1) An accreditation programme so inspection companies' and recyclers' crews sample under our protocol and pay a licence, so the majors distribute us. (2) A lot registry whose receipts lenders advance 85-90% against, for an origination share. (3) An assay-consistent payables index sold to price reporting agencies. (4) Extension to e-scrap boards, catalyst scrap, mixed copper and Ni/Co intermediates.
why_now: Counterparty fear is at a high after the 2025 restructurings, and buyers need a way to attract supply. Black mass flows are being channelled into a bounded, regulated EU/OECD corridor, so a few dozen counterparties and a few hundred lanes can be covered by one house. Escrow and instant-payment rails, e-signature and vault-and-hash registries are now commodity. Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/606 already forces lot-level composition records that the registry can generate.
revenue_model: A take rate of 0.8-1.2% of lot value split between buyer and seller (EUR 1-1.8k on a EUR 150k lot). A pass-through crew fee of EUR 600-900. Small float income. A 0.3-0.5% lender origination share once receipts are financeable. Accreditation licences. Bottom-up: if European black mass trades EUR 0.5-1.5B a year (an estimate, unverified), 1% on a third of it is EUR 2-5M a year before scrap classes beyond black mass. The scale story is the registry and standard, with the lender and index revenue on top. It is a settlement network with float, not a lab.
non_obvious_insight: Inversion: buyers and sellers do not need a smarter referee, they need the decision made before the dispute. Moving the assay of record from ex-post arbitration to an ex-ante release trigger converts a service sold once, in trouble, into infrastructure sold on every lot with a take on GMV. The most credit-challenged recycler is the natural first buyer, because a neutral escrow lets it rent credibility, so the expected resistor is the first to sign. Independence stays the asset, because only a party that neither samples for a side nor holds inventory can be the registry.

title: Pumper-Sampled Hydrogen and Helium Ground-Truth Registry
one_liner: Stop digging through what the industry failed to measure and start measuring it: pay lease pumpers to grab wellhead gas samples, assay them for hydrogen and helium, and build the depth-tagged registry that becomes the standard for what is under the ground.
customer: Wedge: hydrogen, helium and geothermal explorers and their modelers (Koloma-type juniors outside their own acreage, HyTerra/MAX Power-type juniors, Terra AI, HyReveal) who commission sampling campaigns across a fairway. Contributors: small independent operators and the pumpers (lease operators) who visit each well weekly, starting with the Kansas and Oklahoma independents. Later payers: lenders, insurers and resource certifiers who need a standard, auditable measurement before they finance a discovery.
problem: Old well files are noisy for a structural reason: the industry never measured hydrogen or helium. Standard mud-logging and production gas analysis use flame-ionization detectors that cannot see H2 or He, so a 1935 'gas contains 40% hydrogen' note is an accident, contamination and sampling method are unknown, and the parent's archive is capped at about 16,000 free analyses and a 0.5% hit rate. Explorers who need to know where hydrogen and helium are today either drill blind, run private one-off campaigns, or use soil-gas anomalies. Nobody keeps a standardized, depth-tagged, contamination-corrected, fresh measurement for the roughly one million producing US wells or the tens of thousands of new holes drilled each year.
solution: A three-layer business. Layer 1 (first product, sellable in 6 months): buyer-commissioned sampling campaigns. A buyer specifies a transect or 200-well fairway; operators allow their pumpers to fill a $12 sample container at the casinghead or separator vent following a safety protocol; a bounty of about $25 goes to the pumper; samples go to a partner lab or an in-house GC-TCD unit, and the buyer gets H2/He/N2/CO2/Ar/O2/C1-C6 with GPS, photo, chain of custody and an air-contamination correction. Layer 2: a registry with an open measurement spec (sampling method, contamination QC, lab certification) and a contribution scheme: operators get a free full gas assay (which many already pay $50-150 for to support BTU, sales or flaring reports, a hypothesis to test), exclusive rights to their own well results for 90-180 days, and a revenue share. Layer 3: a certified add-on H2/He TCD channel for mud-logging contractors and geothermal drillers so every new hole feeds the registry, and a scoring layer that uses fresh samples to calibrate the archive-based confidence grades from the parent idea.
why_now: Hydrogen and helium explorers are funded (Koloma about $245M, Mantle8 EUR31M, Terra AI $20M with BHP and Khosla, 123 companies per AKAP) but starved of trustworthy labels, and the modelers (Terra AI, HyReveal) explicitly need fresh ground-truth data. Portable micro-GC/TCD analyzers and smartphone chain-of-custody have made distributed sampling cheap, and VLM tools make the old archive a cheap starting prior rather than the product. Geothermal and helium buyers want auditable data for financing, and no standard exists yet, which is the moment a standard can be set.
revenue_model: Sampling campaigns at about $250 per well (cost roughly $60-120 with in-house GC and $130-170 with outside labs); a 200-well campaign is about $50k. Registry subscriptions of $10-50k per basin per year for explorers and modelers. Data licenses to modelers and financiers. Lab certification and channel fees from mud-logging contractors. Optional later: small overriding royalties on leases taken over registry-flagged sections. Year-1 target: 1,500-3,000 wells sampled, 5-8 campaign customers (about $300-400k), 10 registry subscribers.
non_obvious_insight: The right inversion is that data quality, not data availability, is the bottleneck: every archive layer the parent proposed is limited by a measurement nobody made. Because operators pay for gas analysis anyway, the marginal cost of adding H2 and He to a routine sample is almost zero, so the contributor network can be built with a bounty rather than a salesforce. The registry's moat is network economics plus a standard: contributors are also the sources, the modelers need the labels, and lenders will trust the one dataset with certified provenance. Fresh samples also calibrate the archive-derived confidence scores, so the parent idea becomes a cheap prior on top of a proprietary ground-truth set.
first_30_days: Week 1: contract a commercial gas lab that runs GC-TCD (or buy a used micro-GC with TCD for about $15-25k) and design the sample kit and safety protocol with an experienced pumper. Week 2: sign 2 independent operators (about 100 wells each, via the Kansas Independent Oil and Gas Association and personal referrals) on the free-assay, 90-day-exclusive deal. Week 3: sample 100 wells across a transect crossing the Nemaha uplift and publish a one-page ground-truth map. Week 4: pitch 15 juniors and modelers a 200-well campaign at $250 per well with half prepaid, and ask HyReveal and Terra AI for a data-partner letter. Kill test: if no buyer prepays by week 6, sell the same samples as a section-level pack to landmen (see the sharpened offspring).

one_liner: EU retailers and distributors put the desk on their approved-provider list for connected private-label and marketplace products, and their non-EU suppliers pay per SKU family, the way suppliers already pay retailer-nominated test labs, while the retailer gets a live exposure dashboard for its whole connected catalogue.
customer: Mandating party: product-compliance heads at mid-size EU consumer-electronics, DIY, sports (e-bikes), toy and discount retailers and distributors with 50-2,000 connected SKUs, including own-brand ranges. Payers: the 20-200 non-EU suppliers and ODMs behind those SKUs, each paying for the product families it sells to that retailer.
problem: A retailer that sells connected products under its own name is treated as the CRA manufacturer (to confirm with counsel), and an importer or distributor must chase unreachable non-EU suppliers when a vulnerability appears. Retailers have no view of which of their 1,800 connected SKUs contain the component in this morning's exploited-vulnerability headline. Their suppliers will not share firmware willingly and cannot show a 24h capability. The parent's problem is that small makers will not buy a desk they see as insurance. Here the party with the pain is not the party with the budget, and the retailer holds the leverage over the supplier.
solution: Product 1 is a retailer-paid 'Connected Range Exposure Baseline'. The desk collects firmware for 25-50 SKUs, which the retailer can compel from suppliers. It unpacks them, builds the component lists, checks current exposure to KEV/EUVD, tests each supplier's vulnerability-contact deliverability, and delivers a supplier-requirement clause for the next supplier manual. Product 2 is the ongoing service. The retailer's supplier manual names the desk (and any equivalent that passes its audit) as an approved provider. Each supplier enrols product families and the desk becomes its AR and 24/7 filing service, with stack-pooled triage. The retailer sees a live dashboard: for each SKU, affected, not affected or unknown, with supplier response time, supporting delist or recall decisions and its own regulatory file. The desk's fan-out model is reused, but the sales motion is one retailer mandate that brings in many suppliers.
why_now: CRA reporting has been live since 11 Sep 2026 and retailer supplier manuals are being rewritten ahead of Dec 2027. RED delegated-act cybersecurity rules (in force since Aug 2025) and GPSR (since Dec 2024) have already taught retail compliance teams to demand supplier documents and chase non-EU suppliers, so the workflow and budget owner exist. Retail groups have not yet named a vulnerability-reporting provider, so early mandates set the approved list.
revenue_model: Retailer-paid baseline of EUR 10-25k per range as the first sale. Dashboard licence of EUR 15-40k/yr per retailer. Supplier-paid subscription of EUR 600-1,200 per product family per year (falling with volume), plus EUR 1.5-3k per filing event, contractually paid by the supplier. One mid-size retailer with about 150 connected SKU families across 60 suppliers yields roughly EUR 100-130k/yr. Ten retailers gives roughly EUR 1M+ ARR with sales cost amortised across 60 or more payers per mandate.
non_obvious_insight: Change the buyer chain, not the product. Retail supply chains already run on the 'nominated lab' pattern, where the buyer mandates a provider and the supplier pays, and testing spend per product (EN 18031 or similar) dwarfs a EUR 600-1,200 annual desk fee, so suppliers barely resist. The dashboard turns a rare-event insurance product into something a compliance head opens every morning. And retail is the only place where a 24/7 filer has real leverage, because the retailer can delist a supplier that does not respond.
first_30_days: Identify 15 EU retail and distribution product-compliance heads via GPSR, RED and product-safety forums and trade-association events. Pitch each a EUR 12k baseline on 25-50 own-brand SKUs, with the deliverable being an exposure table plus supplier scorecard plus draft supplier-manual clause. Publish the clause as a free template through retail associations to seed demand. Sign 2 paying baselines by day 30-45. Use the baselines to build the first supplier cohorts (20-40 suppliers) and open partnership talks with SGS, Intertek, Bureau Veritas and TUV, who hold the current nominated-lab relationships, about white-labelling the 24/7 back end.
lineage: mutation of I0374 ('Outsourced 24-Hour Vulnerability Reporting Desk (CRA)'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: TridentSec (PSIRT-as-a-Service), Finite State (managed CRA service), Cybellum (managed PSIRT / incident response service), Patchstack (managed CRA Article 14 reporting for open source). White space: The genuinely unserved piece is a contractually guaranteed 24/7 desk that files as the client's named Assigned Representative on the SRP, priced for 20-500 person device makers.
- Nobody found sells this in that form. TridentSec sells operations with no stated 24/7 and no published price. Finite State and H-X draft the notice but leave filing to the customer. Cybellum's service targets enterprises. CVD Portal, CRA Evidence and other tools stop at timers and packages, and their final filing is a human step by the customer. Patchstack files as AR but only for open source, and free.
- The intake step is also unserved: nobody takes weekend and night hits on 'is this KEV/EUVD entry in our firmware' and makes the call inside the 24h window.

What is not white space:
- The SBOM-to-CVE matching layer is commoditised. CVD Portal's Reporting tier is EUR 99/mo, and CRACI, Zealience, Regulus and ONEKEY sell the same thing.
- Boutiques and large consultancies can add 'PSIRT retainer' as a line item in weeks.
- The idea's claim that there is 'almost no visible tooling' is wrong. The service layer is thin, but the tooling layer is crowded.

Structural problems to plan around:
- The CRA fine exemption for micro and small enterprises on the 24h deadline (Art 64(10), https://cra-facts.com/penalties) removes the sharpest fear driver for the smallest customers. The 72h and 14-day deadlines still carry fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover.
- The SRP requires each AR to use a personal EU Login with MFA (https://www.enisa.europa.eu/topics/product-security/single-reporting-platform-srp/frequently-asked-questions), so named analysts must sit in the loop.
- Liability stays with the manufacturer, and the desk needs professional indemnity cover.
- The 24h clock starts when the manufacturer becomes aware, so a desk that spots an exploit may start the client's clock.
- An actively exploited vulnerability in one specific product's components is a low-frequency event. The retainer therefore risks being seen as insurance that customers only buy under audit pressure. | How this version avoids them: None of the competitors in the parent's research sells to retailers. Finite State, Cybellum, CVD Portal, CRA Evidence, EcoComply, H-X and the SBOM vendors all sell to manufacturers one at a time, paying a high customer-acquisition cost per maker, and Patchstack is free and open-source only. One retailer mandate replaces dozens of separate maker sales. The obvious threat is certification bodies and labs, which sell one-off per-model reports while a 24/7 desk has the opposite cost structure, so they are better treated as distribution partners. Switching costs come from integration with the retailer's PLM and supplier-onboarding flow, and from the supplier cohort already enrolled, which a copycat would have to win over from scratch.

title: Hours Exchange: Supply Side of the Work Requirement
one_liner: Invert the wallet: instead of helping people prove hours they already work, build the network of pre-certified nonprofit and public hosts that supply verifiable, flexible community-service and training hours, with insured hosts and signed hour records, paid per active member-month by health systems and plans.
customer: First buyer: population-health, community-benefit and Medicaid-strategy leads at nonprofit and county-owned safety-net health systems. Second buyer: plans. Supply side: 20-50 hosts per county, such as food banks and church pantries, school after-care, libraries, senior centers, community gardens, and clinics' own non-clinical roles. Members: the residual slice of expansion adults who are not exempt, not already working and need hours.
problem: Every product in the parent's competitor set assumes the hours exist and only tracks or verifies them (SteadyIQ, Emmy, the state tracking portals from Maximus, Optum and Acentra, Pointcare, Findhelp). For a member who lost a job or has no hours, no amount of documentation fixes anything. The IFR does count community service, work programs and combined activities toward the 80 hours a month, but there is no supply chain: hosts do not know the state verification standard, cannot supervise flexible 4-hour shifts, lack liability cover, and have no time to produce signed logs. A member 30 days from termination cannot find, book and verify 40 missing hours on their own.
solution: An activity marketplace with a verification rail. (1) Host certification: each host signs a one-page state-format verification protocol (who may sign, what is recorded, non-displacement pledge) and joins a registry that we pre-clear with the state Medicaid agency wherever possible. (2) Micro-shift board: hosts post 3-6 hour shifts (pantry Saturday 8-12), and members claim them by SMS in their language. (3) Verification: check-in and out by phone geofence or supervisor QR or SMS confirmation, producing tamper-evident hour records. (4) Monthly hours letter in the state's format, delivered to the member, the case file and the plan. (5) Master volunteer accident and liability policy plus background checks carried by us, which is the small balance-sheet element and a reason hosts join. (6) Guardrails: the flow starts with an exemption and already-compliant screen, so nobody who qualifies is routed to slots. Participation is voluntary. Later: the same hours count toward SNAP's parallel 80-hour rule (widened by the 2025 law; verify scope), TANF work participation, and court-ordered or scholarship service hours.
why_now: The requirement starts Jan 1, 2027, but the documentation phase is later (an HFMA summary of the IFR says self-attestation is allowed through 2027 and once per beneficiary in 2028). That makes 2027 the year to build the host registry and get states to accept it, before the paperwork wall. The first wave of notices will expose the supply gap, and first movers will hold the hosts and the state relationships. Health systems and plans need a measurable coverage-retention lever for community-benefit and health-related-social-needs spending. Cheap SMS, geofencing and LLM-drafted state-format letters make per-shift verification nearly free.
revenue_model: Health systems or plans pay $20-30 per active member-month (active means at least one verified shift that month). Pilot: about $40k for 150 members over 6 months at roughly $45 per member-month, including host onboarding. Illustrative unit economics: coordinator time $8-10, insurance about $1, SMS and verification about $1, for roughly 50% gross margin. Possible additional flows: SNAP E&T third-party reimbursement (50% federal match on eligible non-federal spending) for host costs where the state plan allows (verify eligibility of this activity), state workforce-board contracts, and later fees from courts and scholarship programs. Bottom-up ceiling, illustrative only: if 1 in 10 of the 2.3M projected FY27 coverage losers (per the HFMA/Applied Policy figure) needs slots, that is 230k people x $240 a year, about $55M a year before SNAP, TANF and court hours.
non_obvious_insight: For the residual slice, the constraint is not proof but the absence of qualifying, supervisable, flexible hours near the member's home. Hosts are short on labor and long on facilities, so this market clears cheaply for whoever supplies the insurance, verification and coordination. Second, a registry-verified, insured host is cheaper for a caseworker to trust than an individual's self-report. Once one state lists registry-verified hosts as accepted evidence, verification cost falls for everyone and the registry becomes the standard, with network economies (hosts and members) and a cornered resource (the state-acceptance record). That is the difference between a tool and infrastructure.
first_30_days: Pick one county in a state that verifies hours early. Ask the state Medicaid agency in writing what a community-service host must sign and record, and whether members can cure by showing current-month hours (the IFR summary says 30 days to demonstrate compliance; test whether that includes hours earned during the window). Get an LOI from one food-bank network covering 10 to 15 pantries as hosts, and quotes for a master volunteer accident policy. Run a manual pilot with 25 members from a clinic's at-risk list using a shared sheet and a Twilio number, and produce real hours letters. Have five conversations with health-system community-benefit leads and price a $40k, 6-month pilot. The 2027 honesty test: do hours letters raise state acceptance versus self-attestation alone?
lineage: mutation of I0573 ('Medicaid Hours Wallet for Gig Workers'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CMS Emmy (Eligibility Made Easy) app and Emmy API, SteadyIQ (Income Passport / Verification Hub), Digital Public Works, Maximus, Optum, Acentra, Deloitte, Gainwell, Conduent, Curam/Merative (state-side community engagement modules). White space: Nobody I found sells an enrollee-side monthly ledger to MCOs or FQHCs that ingests bank, gig and pay-stub data, computes $580 or 80 hours against a state's look-back rules, and produces a state-specific 30-day cure packet. Nothing turned up in searches, CMS vendor pledges or CBPP/KFF/Georgetown landscape coverage. Vendors sit on either side of that gap. State-side vendors (SteadyIQ, Emmy, Maximus, Optum, Deloitte) sell to state agencies. Provider and plan-side vendors (Pointcare, Findhelp, mPulse) sell eligibility monitoring and outreach without gig-income packet building. The clearest unserved segment is workers with no digital trail: cash, informal and 1099-below-threshold workers such as day labor, cleaning and landscaping. Consent-based verification (CBV) via payroll, bank or gig platforms cannot reach them. MCOs may be poor buyers because the IFR bars plans from determining compliance and gives them only a supporting role.
