I could not load the CBPP vendor landscape, the Health Affairs piece or the Federal Register text (all blocked), and I could not confirm what Propel for Plans does or any vendor's funding. | How this version avoids them: SteadyIQ, CMS Emmy, the state tracking modules (Maximus, Optum, Acentra, Deloitte, Gainwell, Conduent, Curam) and Digital Public Works verify or record activity that already exists. Hours Exchange creates and certifies it, and can hand hours letters to those systems as evidence, so they are distribution partners rather than rivals. Pointcare, Findhelp, mPulse, Propel and CareRoute do retention, outreach and information and could list our hosts, but none provides insured, state-format-verified shifts. Findhelp's community-organization network is the closest adjacency, and could add volunteer listings; the response is to own the verification standard and state acceptance, not the directory. General volunteer-management software optimizes engagement, not state-grade verification, insurance and 30-day deadlines, so it is a possible integration rather than a substitute (not researched in the parent's competitor check). The main risk is political optics of 'workfare' and state acceptance, which the exemption-first screen, voluntary participation and non-displacement pledge are designed to manage.

title: Cross-Mine Critical Spares Pool and Inventory Cleanup
one_liner: An AI cleaner for mine SAP materials masters that frees cash from duplicate spares, then turns the informal WhatsApp groups of competing mines' maintenance planners into a contractual, insured rotables pool for mill motors, liners and haul-truck parts.
customer: Supply chain, maintenance and finance heads at mid-size copper and lithium operations, starting in clusters where operators are neighbours: Arizona, Nevada and Utah, Antofagasta, the Arequipa-Moquegua corridor, the Zambian Copperbelt and the Pilbara. They pay a share of freed cash, not an IT budget.
problem: A copper mine holds $30-150M of spares. Materials masters are full of duplicates and near-duplicates (the same bearing under five descriptions), often 20-30% of items, so mines overbuy what is on another shelf. They still stock out on truly critical items (mill drive motors, girth gears, transformers, big castings) with 12-24 month lead times. Meanwhile maintenance planners across competing companies already borrow parts from each other over WhatsApp groups. It works only among friends and has no contracts, insurance, condition guarantees or return terms, so it never scales.
solution: Step one is the wedge. A CSV export of the SAP MM data goes into an LLM pipeline with OEM and aftermarket cross-references, multilingual description normalisation and criticality scoring. It outputs a list of duplicates, surplus and dead stock, plus the freed working capital in dollars. Step two lists surplus and 'insurance spares' on a members-only district board with a standard loan, lease and sale agreement, third-party condition inspection (vibration, NDT), logistics and insurance. It works like airline rotable pooling: three neighbouring mines share one spare mill motor instead of each stocking one.
why_now: Large motors, transformers and castings have longer lead times because of grid and data-centre demand. Steel and copper tariffs make replacement parts pricier. Lithium mines are cash-starved after the price bust, and copper mines face cost inflation and grade decline, so CFOs are hunting working capital. LLMs can now normalise messy multilingual part descriptions at almost no cost, which was not economic three years ago.
revenue_model: 15-25% of freed cash (sales and avoided purchases only, not write-offs), a pool membership subscription ($1-3k per month), and an 8-10% transaction fee on pooled loans and sales, plus inspection and certification fees.
non_obvious_insight: The spares problem is legal and trust-based, not a software problem. The informal swap network is the real supply chain. The biggest saving is not selling dead stock, it is not buying the 'insurance spare' a neighbour already owns. Pooling is an aviation idea that mining has never adopted because competitors will not share data without a neutral third party.
first_30_days: Through ex-colleagues, offer a free 2-week scan of SAP MM exports (CSV) at two or three mid-size mines. Deliver a dollar value of duplicates and surplus and a target list. Sign a success-fee agreement with the first one that shows a big number. In parallel, seed a private 'list before you buy' board among 20 maintenance planners in one district using Signal or WhatsApp, to formalise the network before any software is built.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Verusen, SPARETECH GmbH, SAP (IBP, Store distribution) and IBM Maximo, Partium. White space: Caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted before I could run any queries, so this verdict rests on direct page fetches of known companies. It is not a broad sweep. I could not run forum, Reddit, WhatsApp-group, RFP, Spanish/Portuguese-language or Crunchbase/YC/Product Hunt searches. My 'nobody does cross-company mining pooling' finding is therefore unconfirmed and moderate-confidence.

STEP ONE (SAP dedupe and surplus cleaner) is crowded and should not be the business. Verusen has a live mining case study ($96.8M identified across 17 sites), a listing in the SAP Store, about $33M disclosed funding and enterprise references. SPARETECH does the same dedupe-and-surplus job. Partium and Syniti cover the normalization and SAP-cleansing pieces. The 'LLM cost collapsed, so now it's viable' argument is weak, because Verusen and SPARETECH already do this. The remaining wedge inside step one is small: mid-size mines (roughly $30-150M of spares, one SAP instance, no enterprise budget) below Verusen's Fortune-100 and multi-site-enterprise focus, sold on a success fee. That is a thin, copyable wedge.

STEP TWO (neutral, cross-operator critical-spares pool) is unserved among the players I checked. Verusen's sharing module is intra-company only and has no legal, insurance or inspection layer. Liquidity Services and RB Global sell surplus one-way and offer no loan or lease terms. Grid Assurance proves the pooled long-lead-spares subscription model for utilities, but nobody I found has applied it to mines. The unserved piece is the trust wrapper: a neutral entity, standard loan/lease agreement, third-party condition certification (vibration/NDT), logistics and insurance, and a single-point-of-failure spares register per district.

Risks I could not close out. (1) OEM reman, exchange and consignment programs (haul-truck components, mill liners, motors) are the real substitute for pooling. I could not verify their current terms because the Cat Reman fetch timed out. (2) Competition-law exposure when competing operators share inventory data needs early legal work. (3) The pooled-event frequency is low, so revenue per district is modest, and pooling in Chile or Peru needs local counsel. (4) Verusen could add an inter-company network cheaply; it already lists 'Spare Parts Sharing' and mining customers.

title: Well Covenant Trustee for Rural Data Center Counties
one_liner: A neutral program administrator writes, monitors and runs a county-mandated, developer-funded private-well protection covenant, where excess drawdown versus upgradient control wells triggers in-kind remediation with no lawsuit and no sensor sales.
customer: Wedge: county attorneys and planning directors in rural, private-well counties that are already drafting developer-funded monitoring and neighbor-escrow language (Franklin County IN draft v3.0, Shenandoah County VA, and similar counties in GA, PA and IN). Payer: the independent developer of a 50-500 MW campus in that county, which funds the covenant because the county makes it a permit or development-agreement condition. Not hyperscalers with in-house community teams.
problem: Dry or silted wells are what actually produce lawsuits and hearing revolts (Meta / Newton County GA: neighbors say wells went dry, Meta's own study says groundwater flows away, families sued in Sept 2026). Nobody can separate data-center drawdown from drought or other pumping, so developer-commissioned studies are not believed and neighbor claims cannot be proven. Counties are drafting escrow and monitoring language from scratch, with no tested trigger, no neutral administrator and no legal structure. The parent's sensor-baseline product is a crowded, commoditizing layer (KETOS, Aethair, Envirosuite, consultancies), and its automatic cash payout risks being classed as insurance or read as an admission of liability.
solution: Sell trusteeship of a well covenant, not sensors. (1) A paste-in Covenant Kit for county attorneys: development-agreement rider, trust instrument, enrollment rules, and a published trigger protocol. (2) Trigger design: 8-12 upgradient control wells outside the cone of influence, a 12-month pre-construction regression of each enrolled household well on the control wells, and the developer's metered pumping records shared with the panel. A trigger fires only on sustained deviation beyond the control-adjusted trend (for example >5 ft and >2 standard errors for 30 days), so the developer pays for excess drawdown and not for drought. (3) Remedy is in kind, not cash indemnity: emergency water hauling in 24-48 hours, then pump lowering or well deepening by a pre-qualified local driller at a fixed rate card. The developer is the obligor and a corporate trustee (a regional bank trust department) holds the escrow. We are administrator and data steward and never hold the money. That structure is closer to a remediation trust or warranty than to an insurance policy, and a counsel opinion is the gate. (4) Governance: a 3-person technical panel with one member appointed by the county (ideally from state extension or the geological survey), one by the developer and one by a residents' council. (5) Hardware and labs are bought from KETOS, Eno Scientific, Kunak-type vendors. Noise, PM2.5 and voltage are paid add-ons later.
why_now: Permit politics moved to governors in 2026 (NY Executive Order 62 on July 14, Texas TCEQ permit halt on Sept 21), and counties are writing the rules now. Franklin County's draft already contains developer-paid monitoring wells, a licensed-hydrogeologist assessment and an escrow for 24-hour potable water to impacted neighbors. Shenandoah County officials back applicant-funded third-party testing, and St. Louis's permit requires a developer-funded hydraulic study. Ordinances get copied county to county, so a ready, legally vetted kit written this quarter can become the template. The Newton County lawsuit (Sept 2026) shows what a baseline-less well dispute costs.
revenue_model: Paid by the developer through the county-mandated covenant. Illustrative program of 500 enrolled households: $1,000 per household setup (mostly hardware pass-through, about 25% margin) = $500k; $480 per household per year for telemetry, QA, lab checks and reporting = $240k per year at about 55% gross margin; administrator fee of 1% per year on a $1.5M remediation reserve (about $2,500 per household) = $15k; $500 per adjudicated claim. Extensions add per-household noise, air and voltage modules. Later: license the trigger protocol and dataset to state agencies and insurers. Assumptions to test: expected remedy claim rate of 5-10% of wells over 10 years, and $8-15k per remedy.
non_obvious_insight: The real buyer is the county attorney, not the developer. Because the county imposes the covenant, the developer's objection to volunteering a payout (an implied admission) disappears, and the county gets an instrument it cannot write itself. The economics are also better for developers than the alternative: NorthPoint offered $10k to each of 4,500 households ($45M) and was accused of bribery, while an in-kind covenant reserve for the households that could plausibly lose water is a small fraction of that and is credible because a neutral panel decides. Attribution is fixed in the design (control wells and pumping records), not argued afterward.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: get Franklin County IN's draft v3.0 and the Shenandoah County notes, call the county attorneys and planning directors, and offer to draft the covenant and trust instrument free in exchange for being named in the draft. Days 3-14: retain a land-use or insurance-regulatory lawyer for a written view on insurance characterization (remediation trust, developer as obligor, in-kind remedy); recruit a land-grant extension hydrogeologist and two regional bank trust departments as prospective corporate trustee. Days 10-30: run the parent's 10-neighbor-well pilot in a county with a pending hearing, but with control wells and the regression trigger back-tested on 12 months of public USGS or state well data, and bring the term sheet plus live dashboard to the hearing. Kill gate at 90 days: one developer or county puts a funded escrow in writing and counsel signs off; otherwise stop.
lineage: mutation of I1172 ('Neutral Baselines and Neighbor Guarantees for Data Centers'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: KETOS (SHIELD / KELP data-center water monitoring), Aethair (Aethair PRO, Environet, Thiamis), Envirosuite (ASX:EVS), Kunak. White space: Nobody found sells the bundle, so the status is 'gap' and not 'open'. The sensor and baseline layer is not open: KETOS (about $45M raised) pitches an independent baseline for data centers, Aethair pitches pre-construction baselines, Envirosuite has community dashboards, and consultancies bundle baselines into permitting. The unserved wedge is what sits on top of the sensors. (1) A neutral administrator holding escrowed, tamper-evident data whose governance the county and community accept, unlike developer-hired consultants and unlike opposition-side groups such as CEDS. (2) The Neighbor Guarantee: an automatic, no-litigation payout to households from a developer-funded escrow when a pre-agreed trigger is hit. No vendor, insurer, county ordinance or developer program found does this. The nearest things are Franklin County, Indiana's draft rule (escrow for 24-hour emergency potable water to impacted neighbors, plus developer-funded monitoring wells), one-off buyouts and lump-sum checks. (3) A 10-year, multi-parameter (wells, noise, PM2.5, voltage) record packaged as a permit-condition template that regulators can adopt. Weak points: the sensor baseline will commoditize; attribution is hard, because well drawdown from drought or other pumping is indistinguishable from data-center drawdown unless the design uses upgradient control wells and pumping records; automatic payouts may look like insurance under state law; and developer counsel may resist a pre-committed payout as an admission of liability. Note: the web-search budget ran out before I could check Crunchbase/YC directly for a startup doing exactly the escrow-plus-parametric bundle, so 'nobody found' means no evidence in about 25 searches, not proof of absence. | How this version avoids them: KETOS, Kunak, Eno Scientific, Larson Davis and Clarity become suppliers we buy from, so the sensor layer commoditizing helps our COGS instead of killing the product. Aethair and Envirosuite sell dashboards to whoever pays, not a county-approved covenant with escrow and remedies. TRC, Salas O'Brien and similar consultancies are hired by the developer and are not trusted as neutral, and they do not sell trusteeship or remediation delivery. CEDS sits on the opposition side and cannot be a joint steward. Prevolt and Jambo target stakeholder engagement budgets, not liabilities. Developer checks and buyouts (NorthPoint, Mason County) are lump sums with no evidence layer; we convert that budget into a conditional, audited structure. It is scoped to wells only, where the attribution problem is solvable, so we do not compete in the crowded multi-sensor baseline market.

title: Shared-Aide Pods for 55+ Apartment Buildings
one_liner: One on-site aide team serves 6-10 residents in the same building, delivering assisted-living-style help at a fraction of 1:1 home-care cost.
customer: Owners and operators of independent-living and 55+ apartment buildings (market-rate, senior LIHTC and HUD-202 properties). The payers are middle-income residents and their families, who can't afford $75-130k a year and are stuck on waitlists.
problem: Home care is sold as one aide per client per hour ($35 an hour, about $80k a year for 44 hours a week) only because of legacy billing. Assisted living is at 90% occupancy with almost no new supply before 2030. Residents who age past independent living either move out or go without.
solution: A licensed home-care agency subsidiary (or partnership with one) posts 2-3 aides per shift inside the building. They run scheduled 15-45 minute ADL, medication-reminder, meal-setup and toileting visits, plus overnight response. Dispatch software handles acuity tiers and in-building routing (floors, elevators). Residents buy monthly tiers of about $1,800-3,500, and the property gets a retention amenity.
why_now: NIC MAP shows 57 of 99 metros above 90% occupancy, units under construction at a 2012 low, and no meaningful new supply before 2030. Medicaid HCBS is walled off by 15-month waitlists and labor is scarcer after the 2026 visa pause, so stretching each aide across more clients is the only lever left.
revenue_model: Monthly resident subscription by care tier, with a revenue share or amenity fee to the property owner. Later, Medicaid HCBS or managed-care billing for pods in affordable senior buildings.
non_obvious_insight: Aide hours are cheap to make dense (no drive time, no client-hour minimums) but are priced as if they were mobile. The gap between 1:1 pricing and 1:8 cost is the whole business, and only a property-anchored operator can capture it. Assisted-living-without-the-license is a real category nobody has scaled.
first_30_days: Sign a 90-day pilot with one 100-200 unit 55+ property in a tight market. Subcontract to an existing licensed agency to move quickly, staff a two-aide pod, and target 15 residents at about $2,200 a month. Track aide minutes per resident and move-out avoidance.

Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: National Church Residences (NCR), SASH (Support and Services at Home, Vermont), Selfhelp Community Services (SHASAM), PACE programs (National PACE Association) and PACE-plus-housing projects. I researched only by fetching about 20 known URLs directly and by using prior knowledge. "No scaled startup found" therefore means not found, not verified absent. Rerun 6-8 searches (Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, 'shared aide' and 'cluster care' startup terms) before committing capital.

What looks unserved: (1) A private-pay, tiered, per-building shared-aide subscription in market-rate or workforce 55+ apartment buildings that are not part of a campus. Existing players are either nonprofit coordinator programs (SASH, Selfhelp, NCR), Medicaid or state-licensed programs (PACE, NJ-style ALP), or campus operators (Brookdale). I found no venture-scale company selling this. (2) A dispatch and acuity-tiering software layer for in-building routing (floors, elevators, overnight response). Nothing I fetched showed one.

Serious risks that shrink the white space:
- Licensing. Under Minnesota 144G.08, sleeping accommodations plus any 'assisted living services' (personal care, toileting help, medication reminders, meal setup, safety checks) under contract requires an assisted-living license. Subsidized housing is excluded unless marketed as assisted living, and the statute does not address a property owner that arranges a home-care provider on site. 'Assisted-living-without-the-license' is therefore legally fragile in many states, especially with an owner revenue share and overnight response, which look like 'holding out'.
- Unit economics. Two aides per shift is 17,520 aide-hours a year, about $400-500k loaded at roughly $23-28 an hour. Spread over 15 residents at $2,200 a month ($396k a year) that is break-even at best. At 6-10 residents the cost per resident is about $4,000-5,000 a month, which is above the stated $1,800-3,500 tiers. The idea's own numbers are internally inconsistent (6-10 residents in the one-liner, 15 in the pilot).
- Substitutes. BAYADA and franchise agencies already market to senior-living partners, and NCR and Brookdale could add pods in-house.

title: Revenue-Integrity Diligence for Water System Acquirers
one_liner: The buyer of a small or mid-size water system pays for a 10-day, account-level scan of the target's billing, meters and parcels. It prices hidden revenue and revenue-quality risk before signing, then a success fee on prospectively recovered revenue funds the first-100-days fix.
customer: Corporate development and integration leads at serial acquirers of municipal and small private water and wastewater systems. These are the acquisition teams of investor-owned utilities, PE- and infrastructure-fund-backed water platforms, contract operators bidding O&M or concession deals with revenue share, and regional authorities absorbing failing systems. Deal size is systems with 3k-60k connections.
problem: Buyers price municipal systems on reported revenue and customer counts. Their diligence covers engineering condition, financial audit and legal. Nobody tests account-level billing integrity beyond sampling a few bills. Sellers cannot fix leakage themselves: correcting a meter class, adding unbilled connections or raising a billing floor is politically radioactive for a council, and back-billing is legally capped. So the leakage stays buried until after close. The buyer then discovers it over years, after the price is set, so the buyer neither benefits from knowing it at pricing time nor budgets capex against it. The same blind spot hides negative surprises: estimated reads, stopped meters, dead accounts and customer counts that overstate the base.
solution: Ask the seller's data room for a standard extract: account list, 24-36 months of consumption, meter inventory, rate class and tariff, receivables aging. Join it to the assessor roll, building footprints, permits and public filings. Produce a Revenue Integrity Report in 10 days: (1) a parcels-with-structures versus billed-connections gap by service area; (2) a large-meter low-flow fingerprint ranking accounts by expected annual dollars; (3) read-quality and zero-read audit (estimated reads, stopped meters); (4) misclassified rate class or meter size; (5) a downside adjustment to the revenue baseline; (6) a 100-day plan with a prospective-only fix, a meter test and replacement list, and a price-adjustment memo for negotiations. After close, execute the plan with the buyer's CIS and the field-test subcontractor, and later normalize billing data across the buyer's whole portfolio.
why_now: PFAS, lead-line and aging-pipe capex plus affordability politics push small municipal owners toward selling or regionalizing. Serial acquirers and infrastructure funds are actively rolling up water systems. Fair-market-value sale statutes (for example Pennsylvania's Act 12) have made municipal sales a repeatable process. Diligence windows are short (30-60 days of exclusivity), which fits a 10-day data product. Open footprint data, interval data and LLM-assisted cleaning of messy municipal billing exports make a 10-day turnaround possible for two people.
revenue_model: Fixed diligence fee of $35-75k per target, paid from the deal budget and owed even if the buyer walks. Success fee of 15-20% of verified incremental billed revenue over 24 months post-close (prospective only, verifiable in the buyer's own CIS). Optional 100-day revenue plan retainer of $15k a month. Then a portfolio SaaS tier for serial acquirers: $3-6k per system per year for cross-system revenue-integrity monitoring. Bottom-up assumption: 30-60 diligence engagements a year at about $50k is $1.5-3M of revenue for a small team.
non_obvious_insight: The same $1 of recurring recovered revenue is worth about $1 a year in a city budget, but roughly 8-15x that to an acquirer valuing the system on earnings, and the buyer can bill correctly on day one. Change of ownership is the only moment when meter-class and connection corrections carry no council optics and no back-billing exposure. Payer and problem-owner are misaligned in the parent idea (the city pays for a fight it does not want). Moving the buyer of the utility into the payer seat removes procurement, contingency-ban and optics risk in one step. It also works as an option-free downside screen, which a buyer values on every deal, not only the rich ones.
first_30_days: Build a list of about 40 acquirers from state PUC acquisition dockets, fair-market-value sale filings and municipal sale RFPs. Pick three live or recently announced sale processes. Run a free public-data teaser for each: assessor parcels with structures inside the service area versus service connections in SDWIS and PUC filings, plus the top customers in the seller's annual financial report. Send two-page teasers to corporate development heads. Recruit one advisor, either ex-corporate development at a water utility platform or a water-M&A deal lawyer, for warm intros. Offer a half-price pilot diligence ($15-20k) on one live deal with a data-room extract. Confirm buyers' NDAs allow use of aggregated, anonymized yield data.

There is no public procurement and no contingency-contract exposure, because the payer is a private acquirer.

title: Verified AI Coverage Levels for Vendor Contracts
one_liner: Invert the parent by checking the vendor's insurance from the counterparty's side. AI-enabled vendors upload their policies and get an independent, shareable 'AI Coverage Level' (L0-L3) with monitoring, so enterprise procurement teams can write 'L2 or higher' into contracts. Over time that makes it the insurance-sufficiency standard for AI vendors.
customer: Payer: AI-enabled software and services vendors of 10-300 staff (SaaS with AI features, dev and marketing agencies, MSPs, fintech and health-tech vendors) who sell to banks, health systems and other regulated enterprises with insurance clauses in their MSAs. Free users: enterprise general counsel, TPRM and procurement teams. Later payers: those enterprises' portfolio-monitoring subscriptions, and vendor-compliance and trust-center platforms embedding the check by API.
problem: Enterprise MSAs require vendors to carry, for example, $5M tech E&O and $5M cyber. Proof is a certificate of insurance, which shows limits, carrier and expiry but not exclusions. An absolute AI exclusion in the E&O policy makes the certificate hollow for exactly the failures the buyer worries about (a hallucinated output that costs money, model-vendor data leakage, generated-content IP claims, an autonomous action). The vendor rarely knows, because the broker did not flag the endorsement. The buyer relies on coverage nobody has read, and the indemnity is only as good as the vendor's balance sheet. The insured is the party least motivated to find out its coverage is hollow, so it never gets found. (I could not run web checks in this session to confirm that no COI tracker already reads endorsement wording, so treat that as an assumption to verify first.)
solution: First product, sellable within 6 months: the 'AI Coverage Attestation'. The vendor or its broker uploads the policies and endorsements, and the same diff and classification engine runs. An independent reviewer signs a one-page output. It shows the level and, for four AI failure modes (erroneous output, IP infringement from generated content, data leakage through a model provider, autonomous action), whether each is covered, excluded or silent, plus retro date and whether defence costs sit inside limits. The vendor gets a shareable live link for procurement teams and trust centers. Monitoring re-verifies at every renewal or cancellation and alerts the vendor and anyone who holds the link. The published levels run from L0 (absolute or any-AI exclusion), L1 (gen-AI exclusion with carve-backs), L2 (silent, with no AI exclusion) to L3 (affirmative AI cover). The buyer gets a free portal and an 'AI insurance rider' clause library, so a GC can write 'vendor must hold L2 or higher' into an MSA. Vendors at L0 or L1 are given a neutral list of affirmative markets, but nothing in the model depends on placement.
why_now: Enterprise AI procurement is now standard, and AI addenda in MSAs and security questionnaires are spreading. Vendors renewing on 1 Jan 2027 will be the first large cohort to lose AI coverage silently, just as customers' contracts assume it. Trades Coverage counted 2,369 AI exclusions in force by 31 July 2026, so the exposure exists at scale. Trust-center tools have made 'share evidence by link' the normal way to close security reviews, and AIUC-1 shows that buyers accept an AI assurance standard when it is credible. Long-context extraction over policy PDFs is what makes independent attestation affordable.
revenue_model: Vendor pays $900-2,400 per year per attestation including monitoring, or $250 for a rush one-off when a deal is waiting. Enterprise portfolio monitoring for 200+ vendors is $12-30k per year. Platform API checks are $20-60 each. Affirmative-market referral fees are a later, secondary line. These are estimates to test. The payer is the vendor, because a tick-box that blocks a six-figure deal is worth far more than the fee.
non_obvious_insight: This flips the buyer chain. The party that relies on the coverage, and holds contractual leverage, is the one who can force a hundred vendors to verify, so the value of the credential rises with each buyer that references it. That is a network effect broker software does not have. It also sidesteps the duty-to-advise weakness, because the obligation is contractual, not tort-based. And the level scheme lets an independent attestor become the standard, while carriers cannot credibly grade their own wording and the AI-liability carriers have a conflict.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: interview 20 vendor CFOs and founders and 10 GC or TPRM leads, and collect 5 real security questionnaires or MSAs that contain an AI-insurance question. Days 8-20: run 10 free attestations on real policies from vendors who agree, and publish Levels v0.1 with one redline rider clause. Days 15-30: pre-sell 5 attestations at $500 to vendors with a live deal blocked on the question, and pitch 2 trust-center or COI platforms for a pilot integration. Kill signal: if fewer than 3 of the 20 buyers can name a deal or contract review where the insurance question mattered, the counterparty pull is not there.

This is an independent attestor that routes to them. AIUC-1 is the nearest standard, but it certifies AI-agent controls and is tied to AIUC's own insurance, whereas this rates whether a vendor's existing insurance responds. The free trackers (Gridex, Certian, Vorp Labs, ShadowLock, Trades Coverage) are carrier-level and cannot verify a particular vendor's policy. Adjacent and unverified in this session: COI trackers and trust-center vendors, which I expect to check limits and expiry and not endorsement wording, so a partnership route is likely, and one to check first.

title: Day-Zero Payoff Bridge for Floorplan Dealers
one_liner: Invert the radar: instead of catching dealers who fail to pay the floorplan lender, wire the payoff directly to the lender the day the car sells and get repaid when the retail contract funds, turning sold-out-of-trust risk into a short, fully secured receivable with data-driven underwriting.
customer: Independent and franchised dealers that sell through third-party indirect finance and get squeezed when contracts in transit, stips or unwinds stretch funding beyond the floorplan payoff window. Pilot referral partners are two or three independent floorplan lenders. Capital comes from a credit fund or family-office vehicle buying short-dated receivables. Dealer pays a per-deal fee, and the floorplan lender shares in it and saves audit cost and risk.
problem: SOT often starts as a timing gap, not fraud. The dealer has delivered the car, the retail lender has not yet funded, and the floorplan payoff clock is running. That is why honest and dishonest dealers look identical in the books for a week or more, and it is how a small cash squeeze becomes fraud. Detection tools (including the parent) only tell the lender after the timing gap has already turned into a loss or a phone call. Floorplan lenders then hold reserves and audit constantly because they cannot see the cash in transit.
solution: When a floored car sells, the dealer requests a bridge with the payoff quote, bill of sale and contract or funding-approval docs (LLM-parsed). We verify the sale with the listing signal (retail-sale signature) and cross-check the payoff quote, then wire the payoff directly to the floorplan lender, so cash never touches the dealer and cannot be diverted. We are repaid when the retail lender funds the contract, through a lockbox or deposit-account control agreement, or a notice of assignment where the retail lender allows it. The risk is receivable dilution (an unwound or charged-back contract from a creditworthy obligor), not dealer fraud. Underwriting uses obligor identity, the dealer's payoff-lag history, the dealer's unwind and chargeback record, and the listing check. Rollout runs in three phases. (1) A free dealer-side 'Unpaid VIN clock' built on the radar signal is the top of funnel and lets aged sold-not-paid VINs self-select. (2) A capped concierge bridge of up to $25k per unit. (3) Floorplan lenders name Day-Zero as an approved payoff method, in return for lower reserves and audit frequency, and receivables are sold forward to credit funds so the startup stays capital-light.
why_now: Inventory near 88 days' supply and floorplan at SOFR plus 200 to 400 bps tighten dealer cash. Contracts in transit stretch a week or more. After Sky Auto Mall, lenders have less tolerance for late payoffs. Private credit is searching for short-duration, self-liquidating receivables at high gross yield. LLM document parsing plus listing signals make per-deal verification cheap enough to underwrite $150 fee deals, which was not economical with a human ops desk.
revenue_model: A fee of about 0.5 to 0.7 percent of the payoff per roughly 9-day bridge, which is about 25 percent annualized gross, plus a 10 to 20 percent referral share to the floorplan lender, capital from a credit fund at about SOFR plus 6, and the startup keeping servicing fees and a first-loss or excess-spread slice. Illustration (assumptions): a dealer bridging 15 deals a month at $22k averages about $100k outstanding and pays about $2.1k a month. 5,000 dealers at that size is roughly $500M outstanding, about $125M of gross yield and perhaps $50M to $60M net after capital cost and losses. A $99 to $199 per dealer per month clock subscription is the top-of-funnel product.
non_obvious_insight: The listing-disappearance signal is too noisy to accuse a dealer but precise enough to underwrite a nine-day secured advance, because a false positive costs a declined bridge and not a false fraud allegation. Paying the floorplan lender directly makes the lender's SOT exposure structurally zero for bridged deals, so the lender is a willing distributor and co-subsidizer, and no lender integration is needed at the start because the dealer supplies the payoff quote. Detection was always a workaround for a timing mismatch that capital can simply remove.
first_30_days: Ask two independent floorplan lenders to name their 10 dealers with the most aged, late payoffs for timing reasons and to introduce us. Draft a term sheet with one credit fund or family office for a $500k to $1M pilot facility. Engage commercial-finance counsel on state licensing (some states license commercial lending and receivables purchases). Build the dealer-side Unpaid VIN clock as a landing page plus a manual crawler for the pilot dealers' sites. Aim to sign LOIs with 5 dealers and one capital source, and run the first three concierge bridges by hand to measure dilution, decline and cycle time.

title: Contingency Audit of Unbilled Plumbing Materials
one_liner: Reconcile a trade shop's supply-house invoices against its customer invoices and catch both parts that were bought but never billed and quiet supplier price drift, paid a percentage of what gets recovered.
customer: Plumbing, HVAC and electrical shops doing $1.5-15M in revenue with 5-40 techs, running ServiceTitan, Housecall Pro or Jobber plus QuickBooks, buying on account from Ferguson, Hajoca, Winsupply or a local supply house.
problem: Shops lose margin in two places nobody watches. First, parts go out on a supply-house ticket with a job name, or come off the truck stock, and never make it onto the customer invoice. Techs charge the labor from the flat-rate book and forget the $6 valve, the wax ring, the supply lines, the $40 of fittings. In the shops I know, when the office finally reconciles a quarter it is typically a few percent of revenue. Second, supply houses price off list with a contractor multiplier, and list prices have moved several times since the Section 232 copper, steel and aluminum tariffs (50%, working through a long manufacturer-to-contractor lag). Surcharges appear, job-quoted prices are not honored, returns credits are never issued, and no owner has time to read 40 invoices a week.
solution: Shops set up an email forwarding rule for supply-house invoices and statements and give us read access to their field-service software export. An LLM-based line-item parser ties supply-house lines to jobs and POs, then produces a weekly leak list for the office manager: (1) purchased-not-billed by job, (2) price versus the shop's own multiplier and versus the same SKU 30 days ago, (3) unclaimed return credits, (4) pricebook items where cost has risen past the target markup, with a repricing file ready to import. Later add a benchmark ('you pay 9% more than shops your size for PEX-A fittings') built from pooled anonymized invoices, which is the moat.
why_now: Tariff-driven price volatility means flat-rate pricebooks are stale within a quarter, and owners know it. Invoice parsing with LLMs went from a custom-ML project to an afternoon. Field-service platforms expose APIs and exports. The trades are also ahead of everyone else in adopting software but behind in auditing it, so there is no incumbent audit product.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 25% of recovered and newly captured revenue for the first 12 months (no recovery, no fee), converting to a $199-499 per month subscription for continuous monitoring plus the pricing benchmark. Data licensing of the pooled price index to distributors and manufacturers later.
non_obvious_insight: Owners obsess over lead cost and tech hiring while the highest-ROI dollar is sitting in the shoebox of paid invoices. Everything a tech installs was bought on a ticket with a job name on it, so the truth is already in two systems that have never been compared. This is the freight-audit and telecom-audit model, and no one has brought it to the trades because the people who feel the pain are too busy running trucks to build it.
first_30_days: Offer a free 90-day audit to 10 shop owners from a peer group (a PHCC chapter, Nexstar or Service Roundtable style mastermind). Have them forward statements and give a one-time export. Turn each audit around in 48 hours with a single 'found money' number and a list of specific invoices. Convert the shops with the largest number to the contingency contract. A spreadsheet plus an LLM parsing script is enough for the first ten.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ServiceTitan Accounts Payable (bill inbox, 3-way matching, Manage Statements, Manage Credits, discrepancy flags), Kojo, BuildOps (Procurement and Payables), Fergus. White space: Nobody I found offers a contingency-fee, done-for-you recovery audit for trade shops. What remains unserved is the customer-side leak: parts on a supply-house ticket with a job name, or pulled from truck stock, that never reached the customer invoice, plus supplier price drift and quoted-price violations tied back to the shop's own pricebook and markup targets. Existing tools (ServiceTitan AP, Kojo, BuildOps, Ramp) are software the shop must adopt and operate, and they focus on paying suppliers correctly. Three parts are open: (1) shops on Housecall Pro, Jobber, FieldEdge or Simpro, or ServiceTitan shops not using Procurement/AP, who have no PO-to-job workflow; (2) the done-for-you, no-recovery-no-fee commercial model, which no software vendor offers; (3) a cross-shop SKU price benchmark from pooled supply-house invoices. I found no evidence anyone has assembled that for residential and light-commercial trade shops. ServiceTitan's Manage Statements and Manage Credits are the closest overlap with the returns-credit and price-error pieces.

title: Rural Vet Call Logs as Outbreak Early Warning
one_liner: Producers call the vet before they call the state. Anonymized weekly counts of abortions, maggot wounds, sudden deaths and respiratory clusters are a leading indicator that traders, insurers and packers will pay for.
customer: Buyers: cattle and feeder analytics desks, market advisory and commodity funds, packer and feedlot risk managers, livestock and dairy insurers or reinsurers, animal health company territory teams, and state animal health boards (contracts or grants). Suppliers are participating rural vets, who get free early regional alerts and a small revenue share.
problem: Official disease data lags by weeks because it waits on lab confirmation, and ranchers hesitate to report to the state because a quarantine costs them money. Screwworm was confirmed in a Texas calf in June 2026 after roughly 60 years without a US case, and H5N1 in dairy cattle was spreading for months before detection in 2024. Cattle futures at record prices with a 70-year low herd move violently on rumor, and nobody has a systematic ground-level feed.
solution: A 30-second end-of-week SMS or one-tap tally where each vet reports counts by syndrome (abortion clusters, navel or wound maggots, sudden deaths, neurological, respiratory, milk drops) and ZIP3 or county. Counts are aggregated with k-anonymity (no client identity, minimum practice thresholds) and compared to seasonal baselines. Outputs are a weekly 'Rural Vet Pulse' regional index, push alerts when a region deviates, and an API for institutional subscribers. Vets get the regional alerts free, which is the give-to-get hook.
why_now: New World screwworm has been confirmed in Texas and New Mexico since June 2026, with the first infested horse reported in September 2026, and movement restrictions plus sterile-fly shortages make the outbreak's trajectory the biggest driver of cattle risk. H5N1 in dairy is ongoing, federal animal health staffing is stretched, and academic syndromic surveillance systems exist in Europe (Netherlands, France, Great Britain) but I found no commercial equivalent built from US rural vet practices.
revenue_model: $2-10K per month per institutional data subscriber (analytics desks, insurers, packers), enterprise API tiers, sponsored regional alerts from animal health companies, state or regional government pilots, and a $100-300 per month revenue share to each contributing practice.
non_obvious_insight: Ranchers under-report to the state because reporting costs them money, but they do not hide problems from their vet because they need the vet's drugs and help. The vet's phone is the earliest sensor in the system, and vets cannot share client data but can share counts. Contrarian point: the absence of calls is also a signal, because call volume drops when producers hide problems during a quarantine.
first_30_days: Recruit 25 large-animal practices in Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Kansas and Nebraska through state VMA lists and large-animal vet Facebook groups. Build the weekly tally as a plain SMS survey, with no software integration. Publish a free regional weekly newsletter to the vets as the hook. competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SAVSNET / FAVSNET (University of Liverpool), Morrison Swine Health Monitoring Project (Univ. of Minnesota) and Swine Health Information Center (SHIC), Equine Disease Communication Center (US Equestrian), USDA APHIS / NAHLN and Texas Animal Health Commission (mandatory reporting). White space: Verdict basis: I found no commercial or non-commercial system that turns weekly counts from US large-animal (cattle) vet practices into a regional syndromic index sold to institutional buyers. I could not test that claim against Crunchbase, YC, TechCrunch or Product Hunt, so treat it as unconfirmed on the startup side.

What exists today:
- Academic systems, mostly in Europe (SAVSNET/FAVSNET in the UK).
- A 2025 scoping review of 126 animal syndromic systems: 67 percent were still proof-of-concept, only 20 percent were fully operational, and it noted that even established systems are vulnerable to loss of funding. Operational ones were mostly government run. This is a nearby-review finding, not proof that nobody is building this in the US. Source: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&retmode=xml&id=40327964
- Free industry models such as MSHMP (swine) and the equine EDCC.
- Companion-animal practice data businesses (Animalytix, Vetsource).
- Government mandatory reporting, which now covers confirmed and suspected screwworm within 24 hours in Texas.

Unserved, specifically:
1. Pre-confirmation, syndromic, cattle-specific signals: abortion clusters, maggot wounds, sudden deaths and milk drops, at ZIP3 or county level, weekly. Government reporting only covers confirmed or suspected reportable disease.
2. A denominator and absence-of-calls signal that no current system produces.
3. A decision-grade product for private actors who face NWS movement restrictions and have no ground-level feed: sale barns, order buyers, feedlots, packers, insurers and animal health territory teams.

Structural risks that keep this a gap rather than open:
- Government and free alternatives (TAHC and USDA public case counts, EDCC-style free alerts) satisfy much of the need.
- Vets are legally obligated to report suspects to TAHC, so a private feed adds little for confirmed cases.
- Privacy and trade-implication concerns were the top barrier in an Australian stakeholder study (https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&retmode=xml&id=40037116).
- Selling vet-sourced early disease signals to commodity funds carries legal and ethics exposure (material non-public information, duty-to-report conflicts).

title: Auto Add-On Refund Cascade: Payoff and Return Desk
one_liner: One refund engine for auto add-ons (GAP and service contracts) with two triggers, California's new 3-day return for dealers and the loan payoff for credit unions, sold through the lender who touches both.
customer: California credit unions and regional auto lenders (payoff and indirect-lending departments), who pay for payoff recovery and can introduce their dealer networks. California independent and buy-here-pay-here used-car dealers selling 30-200 cars a month, who pay per return. Later, MGAs and insurers buying return-risk data.
problem: Dealers with no back office must unwind a returned car (lender, add-on administrators, DMV, sales-tax reversal, commissions) inside a very short refund deadline, and fragmented dealers are expensive to reach. Credit unions leave unearned GAP and service-contract refunds unclaimed at payoff because consumer refund sites wait for borrowers to show up. Both jobs depend on knowing what roughly 60 administrators actually require and how fast they pay.
solution: A shared cancellation-cascade engine: administrator playbook and response-time data, a 50-state pro-rata rule set, and generated cancellation packets tracked to payment. Trigger A (dealers): forward the cancellation notice and the desk notifies the lender, submits administrator cancellations, prepares DMV and tax reversals, calculates refund and permitted deductions, and stores the compliance file, at $195-250 per return or a $99 per month standby plan. Trigger B (lenders): free retrospective audit of 500 past payoffs, then $3-6 per payoff or 20-30% of recovered refunds. Pitch the credit union as the channel: 'Your dealers' returns start hitting your payoff desk October 1. We give your dealer network a standby unwind plan, and your members automatic refunds.'
why_now: California's SB 766 takes effect Oct 1, 2026, two days from today, so the first returns arrive within days. No US state has run a mandatory used-car return at this scale. Roughly 3M repossessions a year, 84-month loans and about 30% of trade-ins underwater mean many loans die early with stacked add-ons, and buyers who suddenly cannot afford the payment are the likeliest to return. LLMs can now read messy contract images cheaply.
revenue_model: Per-return fee of $195-250 and $99 per month per-store standby retainer. Credit union payoff fee of $3-6 per payoff or 20-30% of recovered money. Attorney deficiency audits at $99 each. Phase 2: 10-20% of premium as MGA on a $60-120 per used unit return-risk cover. Phase 3: license the cascade workflow to dealer management systems and eContract vendors, and sell administrator refund-speed benchmarks.
non_obvious_insight: These are one business with two triggers. Every California return teaches the desk how each administrator behaves (what they demand, how fast they pay), which makes payoff-refund collections faster and more predictable, and every payoff audit produces the dollar totals that open lender doors. The credit union's indirect dealer network is the only cheap channel to hundreds of small dealers, and the lender is motivated because a dealer's botched unwind becomes the lender's compliance and funding headache. Return and payoff data together also price the return-risk insurance nobody can price today.
first_30_days: Write the cascade checklist for the 20 most common California indirect lenders and 15 administrators. Approach the California Independent Automobile Dealers Association and 10 high-volume independents with the $99 standby plan and a 24-hour turnaround promise. Pitch 3 California credit unions with indirect programs on a free 500-payoff retro audit plus a dealer-network standby offer. Handle the first 20 returns manually with a spreadsheet and e-sign, and log the time and dollar cost of every step.
lineage: hybrid of I0109 + I1151 (Payoff-Triggered Refund Recovery for Credit Unions + Unwind Desk for California's 3-Day Car Return). Why stronger: The lender relationship solves the return desk's distribution problem, and the return desk hands the payoff product a must-have, time-boxed reason to get a meeting. One administrator database serves both, so unit cost falls with volume and collection speed improves. The combined dataset is what makes the return-risk MGA product priceable, which neither parent can reach alone.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Origence (formerly CU Direct) - loan origination/indirect platform (CUDL), Assurant (F&I administrator and TPA), Unverified: consumer GAP/VSC refund-claim services (contingency), Unverified: in-house lender recovery and collections teams and BPO vendors. White space: Verification was limited. The WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted before I could run any queries, and only about 15 direct URL fetches were possible, many of which 404'd or were blocked. That leaves three points.

1. I found no direct competitor selling a payoff-triggered GAP/VSC refund plug-in to credit unions. Origence, the dominant CU indirect-lending platform, and Assurant, a major administrator, show no such product on their homepages.

2. Genuinely unserved and specific, if the market read holds:
   - A per-payoff, lender-integrated refund workflow for dealer-sold, financed add-ons at credit unions.
   - A 50-state pro-rata rules engine combined with an administrator-by-administrator cancellation-requirements database.
   - An attorney-ready audit of repossession deficiency notices that reconciles unearned add-on credits. Consumer-bankruptcy and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid are plausible buyers, because the lender's or dealer's incentive runs against the borrower.

3. Weaknesses in the idea as written, from reasoning rather than found evidence:
   - The claim that the lender never owned the product is shaky. Under many state retail installment sales acts, and under the FTC Holder Rule, the assignee or holder can carry refund and credit obligations. That helps demand, as a compliance and UDAAP driver, but it changes the pitch from 'find hidden money' to 'reduce liability'.
   - A 20-30% success fee taken from a member's own refund has poor fee optics for a credit union. It also conflicts with the idea's own member-experience rationale.
   - On payoff, the refund goes to the borrower, so the CU gets no direct economic benefit. The CU's incentive is goodwill and compliance, not revenue.
   - CU vendor due diligence and core/LOS integration will make the sales cycle slow.
   - The California SB 766 citation in the idea did not check out. The leginfo summary I fetched for the 2023-24 bill described an unrelated social-worker licensing bill. Do not rely on that cite until it is confirmed. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ComplyAuto (exclusively licensed by CNCDA), CDK Global (DMS), CNCDA (California New Car Dealers Association), DealerCenter (DMS for independent dealers). White space: Research limitation: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200), so no searches were run. That means no Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or forum searches, and no search for startups by name. Everything below comes from direct WebFetch of about 30 primary and vendor URLs, with model-generated page summaries. I found NO dedicated 'unwind-as-a-service' for CARS Act cancellations, but I cannot rule out a small startup. Re-run the startup and forum searches before committing.

The idea's premise is weaker than written. Statute text (SB 766, Civ. Code 1784.43, 1784.31(g), 1784.44, as returned by WebFetch and quoted verbatim by the summarizer):
1. The 48-hour duty is only to cancel the contract and refund the buyer. The dealer 'is not responsible for any delays outside the control of the dealer, including delays attributable to the processing of a refund by a bank, credit card company, or other financial institution.' Check payments get a 2-business-day delay. Lender and administrator lag therefore does not create violation exposure. The exposure is the dealer's cash float and its own process failures.
2. The statute lists no duty to cancel service contracts or GAP within 48 hours. The add-on cascade is a business and recovery problem, governed by existing law and contract terms. It is not a statutory deadline.
3. Permitted deductions are formulaic: a restocking fee of 1.5% of price (min $200, max $600), plus $1 per mile over 250 (capped at $150), plus trade-in liens. They are not damage-based. The claim that permitted deductions depend on condition documentation, which justifies the photo and video capture bundle, does not hold up. What does matter is the 400-mile eligibility gate and the trade-in refund rule. If the trade-in is already sold or in title transfer, the refund is the greater of the agreed value, the sale price, or fair market value.
4. Remedies are non-exclusive (1784.22). No explicit private right of action or civil penalty was found. Enforcement runs through DAs, city attorneys and the DMV, plus existing consumer laws.
5. Dealers already run unwinds. California had a 2-day contract cancellation option with a 2-day refund including sales tax (Veh. Code 11713.21), repealed effective Oct 1, 2026. Failed-financing spot-delivery unwinds are also routine (from my background knowledge, not verified here). Buy-here-pay-here lots hold their own paper, so they have no lender cascade at all. The $195 to $250 per-return price competes with a title clerk or F&I manager plus a DMS 'reverse deal' function.

What remains unserved:
(a) Independent, indirect-financed dealers with no back-office bench. Compliance vendors and associations found are aimed at franchised dealers or at pricing, ad and disclosure compliance.
(b) A per-return calculator and checklist: restocking fee, mileage, the trade-in 'greater of three' refund, lender payoff, F&I commission chargeback, and the administrator-by-administrator cancellation basis, with timers and a 2-year compliance file.
(c) Above all, the dealer's economic loss per return. Dealers lost the fee they could charge for the old cancellation option ($75 to $250 or 1%). Restocking is now capped at $200 to $600, against recon, carrying cost and resale loss. Nobody was found pricing or covering that loss.

title: Work-Permit Gap Desk for Frontline Employers
one_liner: Employer-paid, pre-cliff delay suits for workers whose EAD renewals are pending, sold to home-care, nursing and staffing employers as a per-worker maintenance plan instead of a one-off legal purchase.
customer: HR and compliance directors or owners of 150-1,500 employee home-care agencies, skilled-nursing operators and staffing firms in the NYC-metro and New Jersey area (workers resident in E.D.N.Y., S.D.N.Y. and D.N.J., where delay suits most often end in agency action), each with hundreds of workers on time-limited work authorization (asylum-pending, adjustment-pending, parole and DACA categories). The worker is the lawyer's client; the employer is the payer and the buyer of the platform. Later channel: I-9/E-Verify vendors, PEOs and state home-care and staffing associations.
problem: Employers eat the cliff. Since the 540-day automatic EAD extension ended for renewals filed from late Oct 2025, a worker whose I-765 renewal is still pending on the expiry date must come off the schedule. A care agency watches a predictable slice of its workforce disappear for months, pays replacement and onboarding costs, and has no lever to pull. Its HR team already tracks every expiry date for I-9 compliance, but that process ends at 'alert' with no remedy step. Immigration counsel are hired by individuals or for petitions like H-1B and PERM, never as an operations service for frontline workforces, so this problem has no owner.
solution: Gap Desk in three parts. (1) Free EAD Gap Calculator: HR uploads employee ID, EAD category code and expiry date (no names), and gets the projected number of workers who will hit expiry before a decision, priced in lost margin and replacement cost. (2) Enrolled program: the employer offers a voluntary benefit to every employee with time-limited work authorization regardless of nationality (to limit anti-discrimination exposure). The platform watches filing date against expiry; when a ledger-set trigger fires (case beyond posted time and expiry approaching), it obtains the worker's consent and files through a panel of federal-admitted attorneys at a flat fee. Structure: the worker is the client, the employer pays as a third-party payer with informed consent (independent judgment and confidentiality preserved), and the employer sees only a status date. (3) Bridge kit: job-hold and leave templates and a reinstatement re-verification checklist so the employer keeps the seat during the gap. Out of scope by design: TPS terminations, revoked parole and denials, which are not delay problems.
why_now: The auto-extension ended in Oct 2025, and Mandamus.com's case-law tracker calls I-765 mandamus a 'primary remedy' since then, so the cliff is new and the remedy is proven. Expiry dates are known 6-12 months ahead, so the risk is forecastable. Care-sector labor is scarce, making each lost seat expensive. LLM drafting plus a per-district ledger lets a panel attorney turn a routine I-765 suit in about an hour, making a $1,750 flat fee profitable. The USAO's 45-90 day resolution pattern matches the length of a typical gap.
revenue_model: Employer pays $5 per covered worker per month (monitoring, calculator, case management) plus $2,000 per triggered case: $1,750 paid directly to the panel attorney and $250 to the platform as a flat administrative fee. Never a percentage of the legal fee. Illustration for a 400-worker agency: $24k/year subscription plus about 20 triggered cases (about $5k platform, $35k to attorneys). Assumption to validate in pilots: a 90-day gap costs an agency roughly $5-10k in lost margin and replacement, so 20 avoided gaps clearly exceed the roughly $59k program cost. Year 2: I-9 vendors and PEOs resell for a cut of the subscription only.
non_obvious_insight: The party with the most to lose from a stuck case is the employer, yet employers have never been the buyer because immigration law treats the individual as the client; third-party payer rules allow the employer to pay while the worker stays the client. Once the employer pays, the product changes character: expiry dates are known a year ahead, so demand is a forecastable renewal calendar and recurring subscription instead of lumpy, panicked legal purchases. And the employer's I-9 tickler is already the distribution asset, since it holds exactly the dates that trigger the suit.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: build the calculator as a spreadsheet plus web form and run it on anonymized expiry lists from 3 friendly employers. Days 1-10: sign 2-3 panel attorneys admitted in E.D.N.Y., S.D.N.Y. and D.N.J. at $1,750 flat and get an employment-law read on third-party-payer, anti-discrimination and prepaid-legal-plan rules. Days 7-30: contact about 60 NYC-metro and NJ home-care agencies and staffing firms through state association events and LinkedIn, lead with their own calculator output, and close 3 paid pilots at about $2,500/month concierge plus per-case fees. Go/no-go: at least one employer with a real expiring cohort authorizes a filing within 30 days, and outcomes are logged to seed the ledger.

The open data (CourtListener) and free guides make the raw ingredients cheap for anyone.

Conn., DNJ and EDMI at 83-85% voluntary dismissal after agency action).

Parts of the pitch look weak against what I found:
(1) Nationality-hold suits look poor. Per Mandamus.com's summary of 13 D.D.C. delay decisions from June to August 2026, the government won all 13. Judge Leon in the consolidated Ivanov case found the categorical pause unexplained but dismissed the delay and mandamus counts under TRAC and limited relief to named plaintiffs. A 'nationality hold' template is a liability, not a hook.
(2) S.D. Tex., one of the five launch districts, is hostile. Cheejati v. Blinken (5th Cir. 2024) bars I-485 delay claims on jurisdictional grounds, and DOJ there files motions to dismiss rather than negotiate.
(3) Buckhannon: when USCIS simply adjudicates, the plaintiff is not a prevailing party and can't recover EAJA fees (typically $4,000-$12,000 only if a consent order is obtained). The flat fee holds up, but the 'forced deadline' product should be structured around consent orders.
(4) The '6-10 hour learning curve' is being eroded by free content and general AI drafting.
(5) The data moat is thin. CourtListener docket data is free, and the boutique firms already publish their own district stats. | How this version avoids them: Mandamus.com sells single suits to individuals at $5,000 with SEO funnels and cannot run a workforce calendar for an employer. I-9/E-Verify vendors track expiry dates but stop at an alert (not verified in this research); they are channel partners, not rivals. Docketwise and Boundless serve firms and individuals on petitions, not employer-paid remedies. Alma sells O-1/EB-1 strategy to companies for high-skill hires, not frontline EAD renewals. Large corporate immigration firms serve professionals where ticket sizes are big; a $1,750 frontline case is below their radar (unverified). DoNotPay and free pro se guides cannot give an employer a managed, attorney-signed service with status reporting. Employer ownership of the buyer relationship is the wedge none of them hold.

title: Carve-Out Audit Kit for Challenger ASC Billers
one_liner: A white-label implant carve-out engine for independent ASC billing companies, who use a free lookback on a prospect or new client as their sales weapon and split the recovered dollars with us.
customer: Independent ASC billing and RCM companies with roughly 8-60 ASC clients. These are the long tail behind SIS/Surgical Notes, National Medical Billing Services and Nimble. The buyer is the owner or head of sales. The ASC still pays the fee, but through its biller.
problem: Billers win ASC clients on percentage fee and references, and the new-ASC wave makes that fight harder. They can't afford implant analysts or invoice-parsing tooling for 30 clients. A startup selling direct to ASCs hits a trust wall, because owners won't hand 835s and contracts to an unknown vendor. Billers already hold the BAAs, the ERA feeds and the contract PDFs. Billers also don't buy 'recovery', because it admits past misses. They buy client acquisition and retention.
solution: White-label 'Carve-Out Desk' with three parts. (1) Lookback as an RFP weapon. For a prospect, or a new client in its first 30 days, ingest 12-24 months of 835s, implant log and AP invoices and return a co-branded Carve-Out Leak Report showing dollars by payer and CPT. The new biller can recover the prior biller's misses with no political cost. (2) Recovery ops. We prepare attachment packets and corrected claims and appeals, and the biller submits, or we do so under the biller's credentials. (3) A prospective pre-bill gate, delivered as upload plus a review queue that works with whichever PM system the biller's clients use, checking invoice attached and L8699/027x coded to trigger the carve-out. Each partner audit adds payer-clause entries to a shared clause library.
why_now: New and converting spine and ortho ASCs are choosing billers now, as CMS's CY2026 ASC rule (CMS-1834-FC) reportedly expands the ASC list; verify the exact list. Payer AI payment integrity makes attachment mistakes costly. Invoice parsing now costs cents, so the audit can be run for a prospect who has not yet signed. Becker's coverage in 2026 shows implant cost is the hot ASC topic, so billers have a live sales angle.
revenue_model: Money flow: the payer pays the ASC as usual. The ASC pays the biller 25-30% of recovered carve-out dollars under a 'Carve-Out Assurance' schedule the biller adds to its contract. The biller remits about 50-60% of that to us, so we take roughly 15% of recovered dollars and the biller keeps roughly 10-12% for near-zero labor. On top, $300-600 per facility per month for the pre-bill gate and a $2-4k flat fee per prospect lookback, credited against the rev-share. Illustrative unit economics, to be verified in pilots: a facility recovering $240k in year one yields about $36k to us plus about $6k of platform fees. Twenty partners with an average of 20 implant-heavy clients each is 400 facilities, which supports a $5-10M ARR outcome.
non_obvious_insight: The biller's incentives are the opposite of the ASC's. Incumbents will not audit themselves, but their challengers desperately want a proof-of-value opener. The moment of highest willingness to pay is a biller switch or a new ASC opening, because the prior party's misses can be recovered with no blame. The channel also removes the hardest part of direct sales: data access and trust arrive through an existing BAA chain. Every partner lookback grows the cross-client clause library, and an incumbent biller who refuses the tool becomes exposed to challengers who use it.
first_30_days: Build a list of about 150-200 independent ASC billers from ASCA and state ASC association vendor directories, Becker's ASC sponsor lists and LinkedIn. Pitch 40 owners by phone with one offer: 'Give me one prospect you're pitching, or your newest client, and I'll return a co-branded carve-out leak report in 10 days, free.' Convert 3 pilots with 2 audits each, run by hand with a coder and a spreadsheet plus an LLM for invoices. Success: at least $100k of collectible carve-out dollars found on 2 of 3 audits, and one biller signing the rev-share and the Carve-Out Assurance add-on. Kill signal: billers say they already catch this and the reports show under 2% leakage. In that case pivot to selling direct to in-house-billing ASCs.

- I could not verify the CY2026 IPO-list phase-out and ASC list additions cited in the idea's why-now. CMS's page confirms only that a CY2026 ASC final rule (CMS-1834-FC) exists. | How this version avoids them: It does not fight SIS/Surgical Notes, NMBS or Nimble head-on. It sells to their challengers and gives them a weapon the incumbents' scale doesn't cover. Aspirion, FinThrive, Sift and Waystar are enterprise tools for health systems and contingency recoverers that would compete with billers on recovery, so billers won't buy or partner with them. Aspirion could add carve-outs, but it would sell to ASCs directly and cannot use a biller channel without cannibalizing its own contingency model. HST Pathways and SIS software hold the inventory data but are tied to their own PM platforms, while this kit is PM-agnostic, and they can be data sources rather than rivals. title: Canary Humans: Leak-Testing ID Verification Vendors
one_liner: Put consenting, instrumented real people through a platform's ID and age checks, then prove whether the vendor kept, leaked or resold their documents.
customer: Trust-and-safety, privacy and vendor-risk leads at platforms that outsource ID or age checks (dating apps, gig and rental marketplaces, cannabis and vape retail tech, crypto exchanges, adult and gaming operators), and the cyber insurers underwriting them.
problem: Platforms pick verification vendors on a SOC 2 badge and a promise to delete images quickly, and customers cannot test that promise. AU10TIX, Discord's support vendor, Persona and IDScan were all breached in 2024-26. IDScan reported 150M+ licence scans stolen in Sept 2026. Ofcom and state AGs judge platforms on 'reasonable steps', so the platform owns its vendor's failure.
solution: Recruit a few hundred paid 'canary humans' with unique emails, phones, addresses and ID numbers, and enrol them in the customer's live verification flow with the customer's consent. Then run scheduled tests: deletion requests, access requests to the vendor and its sub-processors, and monitoring of breach dumps, data-broker files, phishing and spam lists and dark-market listings for canary-unique strings. The deliverable is a quarterly retention and leakage attestation with evidence, usable in vendor contracts, cyber-insurance applications and regulator files. It also produces a public 'retention half-life' benchmark by vendor.
why_now: IDScan's Sept 2026 breach (150M+ licences) and the Persona, AU10TIX and Discord-vendor incidents showed that certified vendors leak. The EU's 31 Dec 2026 age-verification rollout deadline will push thousands more sites to outsource checks. Ofcom has opened 90+ investigations and issued fines. The Delve scandal (Mar-Apr 2026) showed that paper compliance is not proof.
revenue_model: $25-100k per year per platform per vendor tested, an insurer portfolio programme (per-insured fee), and a breach-forensics retainer. Later add an efficacy-proof product for privacy-removal services.
non_obvious_insight: Compliance automation (Vanta is at roughly $300M ARR) certifies that controls exist on paper, and nobody tests outcomes. A verifier's product is a promise to forget, and the only way to audit a promise about data is to plant traceable data and watch where it surfaces. Security calls these honeytokens and direct marketers call them seed lists, but nobody has applied the trick to verification vendors.
first_30_days: Recruit 50 privacy-minded volunteers at $100-200 each with signed consent and a legal review (no fake IDs, real people only). Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Vanta (compliance automation), SecurityScorecard, Transcend (privacy/DSR orchestration), Age Check Certification Scheme (ACCS) and Age Verification Providers Association (AVPA) standards ecosystem. White space: Research limits first. WebSearch hit its 200-call session cap before I could run any of the planned startup, Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt searches, so I did not verify the absence of a direct startup. I used WebFetch on named pages and GitHub repo searches instead. Wikipedia and vendor-site fetches turned up no company that recruits real, consenting individuals, enrols them in a platform's live ID or age-check flow, files deletion and access requests with the vendor and its sub-processors, watches for the canary strings, and issues an attestation. GitHub searches for open-source tools returned nothing relevant.

What is unserved: outcome-based, adversarial proof of the promise to forget. Incumbents cover the adjacent layers.
- Compliance automation (Vanta) covers whether controls exist on paper.
- Standards bodies (ACCS, Kantara, AVPA/ISO 27566) cover process and control audits.
- SecurityScorecard covers passive outside-in ratings.
- DSR orchestration (Transcend) covers a customer's own deletions.
- Honeytoken vendors cover a customer's own intrusions.
- HIBP-style monitors cover leaked-string detection.

The specific unserved piece is an independent, real-human, live-flow test with a public per-vendor retention benchmark.

Structural weaknesses of the pitch:
- Real government ID numbers cannot be unique canaries. Only emails, phones, addresses and name variants are. Leak detection depends on those fields surfacing in dumps, and image-only dumps are hard to search.
- The base rate of any given vendor leaking in a quarter is low. Most attestations would say nothing found, which is weak evidence. Retention and deletion behaviour, tested through DSARs and access requests, is the part canaries can actually prove.
- Vendors may treat the enrolments as terms-of-service violations. Customer consent helps but does not remove that risk.
- Privacy-preserving designs such as on-device age estimation and reusable digital ID could shrink the retention problem that this idea audits.
